why.correct: Branches of the coronary arteries dive into the myocardium. In systole the contracting muscle, especially in the thick left ventricle wall, compresses those vessels and slows flow. In diastole the muscle relaxes, the vessels open, and most flow occurs.
options: The coronary artery openings do not close. The limit on flow comes from the vessels inside the wall being squeezed.
Blood in the chamber reaches only a thin inner layer of muscle next to the endocardium. The rest of the wall depends on the coronary arteries.
Correct. The muscle compresses its own vessels as it contracts, like squeezing a garden hose.
Heart muscle uses oxygen all the time, and most of all while it contracts. Its supply, not its use, is what falls in systole.

why.correct: The mitral valve is the left atrioventricular valve, between the left atrium and the left ventricle.
options: Correct. Blood crosses the mitral valve from the left atrium into the left ventricle.
The tricuspid valve lies on the right side, between the right atrium and the right ventricle.
The pulmonary valve guards the exit from the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk.
The coronary sinus is a vein on the back of the heart that drains the heart wall into the right atrium, not a valve.

why.correct: At rest, tissues take only about a quarter of the oxygen that arrives, so returning blood is still about 75 percent loaded. It is dark red. Veins look blue through the skin because of how skin scatters and absorbs light.
options: No blood in the body is blue, whatever its oxygen content.
Deoxygenated blood still carries a lot of oxygen; at rest the tissues remove only about a quarter of it.
Correct. Deoxygenated blood is dark red and still carries most of its oxygen at rest.
Bright red, fully loaded blood is oxygenated blood leaving the lungs, not blood returning in a vein from the hand.

why.correct: The heart has small anastomoses between coronary branches. When an artery narrows slowly, more blood is pushed through these connections and they widen over months, forming collateral circulation. When the artery finally closes, collaterals can still feed much of the region. Patient B had no time to develop them.
options: Correct. Slow narrowing drives collateral circulation to develop through anastomoses.
Heart muscle depends on aerobic respiration and cannot switch to working without oxygen for long, however slowly a block develops.
Veins carry blood away from the heart muscle. They do not reverse and supply it.
In a healthy adult heart the interventricular septum is a solid wall, and even if blood crossed it, it would not reach the blocked artery's territory.

why.correct: The coronary sinus lies in the coronary sulcus on the back of the heart. The great, middle, small and posterior cardiac veins empty into it, and it empties into the right atrium.
options: The great cardiac vein empties into the coronary sinus. It is one of its tributaries, not the wide collecting vein itself.
The inferior vena cava enters the right atrium from below and drains the lower body, not the heart wall.
Correct. This is the coronary sinus.
The posterior interventricular artery runs down the groove between the ventricles on the back. It is an artery, not a collecting vein in the groove around the heart.

why.correct: The pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs into the left atrium. They are veins because they carry blood toward the heart.
options: The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the right ventricle to the lungs.
The aorta carries oxygenated blood away from the left ventricle to the body.
The venae cavae return deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium.
Correct. These are the pulmonary veins.

why.correct: One cycle lasts 60 s ÷ 50 beats = 1.2 s. Subtract systole: 1.2 s − 0.3 s = 0.9 s of diastole.
options: 0.5 seconds is the diastole for a heart rate of 75 beats per minute, when each cycle lasts 0.8 seconds.
0.3 seconds is the length of systole, not diastole.
1.2 seconds is the whole cycle. Systole still has to be subtracted.
Correct. 1.2 s per cycle minus 0.3 s of systole leaves 0.9 s.

why.correct: In this pattern, the back of both ventricles is fed by a branch of the circumflex artery, which comes from the left coronary artery. A block of the left coronary artery before it branches cuts off the circumflex, and so the posterior interventricular artery too.
options: In this person the right coronary artery does not give rise to the posterior interventricular artery, so a block there would spare the back of the ventricles.
Correct. The left coronary artery feeds the circumflex, which here feeds the posterior interventricular artery.
The marginal arteries feed the right edge of the heart, not the back of both ventricles.
The coronary sinus is a vein that drains blood away. Blocking it does not stop arterial supply to the back of the ventricles.

why.correct: Flow depends on the pressure difference and the resistance. The pulmonary circuit's vessels are short, wide and numerous, so they resist flow little, and a small pressure moves the full volume. The systemic vessels resist much more, so the left ventricle needs about 120 mm Hg.
options: Correct. Low resistance in the pulmonary circuit means a small pressure moves the same volume.
Distance matters only through resistance. Pressure still drives flow in both circuits; the lungs simply resist it less.
Oxygen content does not noticeably change how thick blood is. The same blood flows through both circuits.
Valves only let blood through in one direction. They do not add pressure.

why.correct: Starved muscle fibers cannot run aerobic respiration fully, so they make less ATP and shift to anaerobic metabolism, producing lactate. Lactate, other acids and chemicals from the ischemic muscle stimulate pain-sensing nerve endings.
options: Correct. Ischemia leads to lactate and other chemicals, which stimulate pain nerve endings.
A blocked artery does not stretch or tear the pericardium. The pain comes from the starved muscle itself.
A coronary block does not simply stop the heartbeat, and the pain comes from chemicals released by ischemic muscle, not from the heart pausing.
A blocked artery lowers, not raises, the oxygen reaching the muscle downstream.

why.correct: The coronary arteries are the first branches of the aorta. The left coronary artery gives off the anterior interventricular artery, which feeds capillaries in the front wall of the left ventricle. The great cardiac vein collects that blood and empties into the coronary sinus, which drains into the right atrium.
options: The left coronary artery leaves the aorta just above the aortic valve. It is short and splits almost at once.
The anterior interventricular artery is one of its two branches and runs down the front of the heart.
Its branches dive into the myocardium and end in capillaries, where oxygen leaves the blood.
The great cardiac vein runs up beside the anterior interventricular artery and collects that blood.
The great cardiac vein empties into the coronary sinus on the back of the heart.
The coronary sinus empties into the right atrium, which ends the loop.

why.correct: In systemic capillaries, cells use oxygen and make carbon dioxide, so oxygen moves down its gradient out of the blood and carbon dioxide moves into it. At rest the tissue takes only about a quarter of the oxygen.
options: Yes. Cells use oxygen, so it is lower in the tissue and diffuses out of the blood.
Yes. Cells make carbon dioxide, so it is higher in the tissue and diffuses into the blood.
No. Oxygen moves into the blood in the pulmonary capillaries, not in the tissues.
Yes. At rest, blood leaving the tissues is still about 75 percent loaded with oxygen.
No. Carbon dioxide moves out of the blood in the lungs, where it is lower in the air of the alveoli than in the blood.

why.correct: At threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium rushes in down its electrochemical gradient, taking the membrane from about −70 mV to about +20 mV in about a millisecond. This is the same fast upstroke as in neurons and skeletal muscle.
options: L-type calcium channels open too slowly to carry a millisecond-long upstroke. Calcium entry holds the plateau that follows.
Correct. Fast sodium entry carries phase 0.
Potassium leaving makes the inside more negative. It carries repolarization in phase 3, not the upstroke.
Calcium released from the SR goes into the cytosol, not across the plasma membrane, so it does not change the membrane potential's upstroke. It activates contraction.

why.correct: During the plateau, L-type calcium channels let positive charge in as calcium while potassium channels let positive charge out as potassium. The two currents nearly cancel, so the voltage barely changes.
options: The sodium channels inactivate within a millisecond or two of the upstroke and stay inactivated through the plateau.
Ions are moving in both directions throughout the plateau. The voltage is flat because the movements balance, not because they stop.
The sodium–potassium pump runs throughout. Its small current does not create the plateau.
Correct. Inward calcium current roughly equals outward potassium current.

why.correct: Blocking L-type channels shrinks the calcium trigger, so calcium-induced calcium release falls and each contraction weakens. The sodium upstroke is unaffected.

variables.name: Calcium entering the cell during the plateau
variables.why: The blocked L-type channels are the path calcium takes into the cell during the plateau, so less enters.

variables.name: Calcium released by the sarcoplasmic reticulum each beat
variables.why: Entering calcium is the trigger that opens the SR's release channels, so a smaller trigger opens fewer of them and less calcium is released.

variables.name: Force of each contraction
variables.why: Less calcium in the cytosol binds less troponin, so fewer cross-bridges form and each contraction is weaker.

variables.name: Height of the phase 0 upstroke
variables.why: The upstroke is carried by sodium through voltage-gated sodium channels, which the drug does not block.

why.correct: Raising extracellular calcium steepens the gradient for calcium entry, so more calcium flows in through the channels that are still open. The larger trigger opens more SR release channels, more calcium reaches troponin, and more cross-bridges form.
options: Correct. More calcium entering means a larger trigger for calcium-induced calcium release.
Calcium in the blood does not strengthen the sodium upstroke, and the upstroke does not set the force of contraction.
The SR's release channels face the cytosol, not the blood. Calcium from the blood has to enter the cell first, through L-type channels.
A longer refractory period would not strengthen contraction; force depends on how much calcium reaches troponin.

why.correct: Charge from a neighbor brings the cell to threshold; the sodium upstroke depolarizes it; depolarization opens L-type channels; entering calcium opens the SR's release channels; the SR floods the cytosol with calcium; calcium binds troponin and the cell contracts.
options: The action potential reaches the cell as charge from a neighbor that has already fired.
That charge depolarizes the cell to threshold, and voltage-gated sodium channels open for the upstroke.
The depolarization slowly opens L-type calcium channels, and calcium enters during the plateau.
The entering calcium crosses a narrow gap and opens the SR's calcium release channels.
The SR releases far more calcium than entered: calcium-induced calcium release.
Calcium binding troponin moves tropomyosin aside, and cross-bridges form.

why.correct: The sodium channels stay inactivated through the whole plateau, so the absolute refractory period lasts about 200 to 250 ms, nearly as long as the contraction. No new action potential can start until the cell is already relaxing, so twitches cannot add up into tetanus.
options: Correct. The long refractory period prevents wave summation and tetanus.
Even with a smaller SR, cardiac muscle cells get enough calcium for strong contractions. The limit is electrical, not a shortage of calcium.
Fast spread through gap junctions does not stop a cell from being restimulated. What stops it is that the cell cannot fire again until its refractory period ends.
Heart muscle makes ATP continuously by aerobic respiration. The lack of tetanus comes from the refractory period, not from an ATP limit.

why.correct: Intercalated discs join cardiac muscle cells end to end. Each disc holds desmosomes and gap junctions.
options: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a network of membrane sacs inside each cell that stores calcium. It does not join two cells.
The sarcolemma is the plasma membrane of each cell. An intercalated disc is where two cells' membranes meet and are joined.
A T tubule is an inward fold of the sarcolemma that carries the action potential into the cell, not a junction between cells.
Correct. This is an intercalated disc.

why.correct: Gap junctions are clusters of channels that link the cytoplasm of two neighboring cells, so ions and charge pass directly from one to the other.
options: Desmosomes anchor the two cells together mechanically. They do not form channels between them.
Tight junctions seal the spaces between epithelial cells. They are not the channels in cardiac intercalated discs.
Correct. Gap junctions connect the two cells' cytoplasm.
The intercalated disc is the whole junction. The pin marks one kind of junction within it.

why.correct: A contractile cell fires only when charge from a neighbor brings it to threshold. That charge travels through gap junctions. With them closed, the charge cannot pass, so the neighbors stay at rest.
options: Closing gap junctions does not change a cell's threshold. It stops the charge that would reach it.
If a neighbor did fire, its own L-type channels would still produce a plateau. The problem is that it never reaches threshold.
Correct. Without gap junctions, the action potential cannot spread from cell to cell.
The first cell's own channels still work, so it repolarizes normally when its potassium channels open.

why.correct: Midway through the plateau, calcium enters through open L-type channels while potassium leaves, keeping the membrane near 0 mV. The sodium channels are inactivated, which is why the cell is refractory.
options: Yes. Calcium entering through L-type channels holds the plateau.
Yes. Potassium leaving roughly balances the calcium entering.
Yes. The sodium channels inactivated just after the upstroke and stay that way while the membrane is depolarized.
No. The membrane is near 0 mV during the plateau. It is near −90 mV at rest.
No. Inactivated sodium channels cannot reopen until the membrane repolarizes, so the cell is in its absolute refractory period.

why.correct: Phase 3 repolarization is carried by potassium leaving the cell, as the L-type calcium channels close and more potassium channels open. Calcium does not rush out through channels; it is removed slowly by pumps and an exchanger.
options: This step is correct. At rest, potassium leak channels hold the membrane near −90 mV.
This step is correct. Fast sodium entry carries the upstroke.
This step is correct. A brief potassium current makes the small notch after the peak.
This step is correct. Balanced calcium entry and potassium exit hold the plateau.
This is the wrong step. Potassium leaving, not calcium, repolarizes the membrane in phase 3.

why.correct: Phase 2 is the plateau. Calcium entering through L-type channels balances potassium leaving, and the membrane stays near 0 mV for about 200 ms.
options: The membrane stays near 0 mV in phase 2. It does not go below the resting potential.
Sodium channels stay inactivated through the plateau. They recover only as the membrane repolarizes in phase 3.
Correct. The plateau follows the notch.
There is only one sodium upstroke. The sodium channels are inactivated during phase 2.

why.correct: The shortest possible time between upstrokes is 0.2 s. That gives 1 ÷ 0.2 s = 5 per second, and 5 × 60 = 300 per minute.
options: 200 is the refractory period in milliseconds, not a rate.
Correct. 5 per second times 60 seconds is 300 per minute.
500 per minute would mean one action potential every 0.12 s, which is shorter than this cell's 0.2 s refractory period allows.
120 per minute would mean one action potential every 0.5 s, far slower than the refractory period allows.

why.correct: Blocking the repolarizing potassium channels prolongs the plateau, which keeps the sodium channels inactivated longer, lengthening the refractory period and lowering the maximum firing rate.

variables.name: Duration of the action potential
variables.why: With less potassium leaving, outward current takes longer to overcome calcium entry, so the plateau lasts longer and repolarization is slower.

variables.name: Length of the absolute refractory period
variables.why: The sodium channels stay inactivated as long as the membrane stays depolarized, so a longer action potential means a longer refractory period.

variables.name: Fastest possible rate of action potentials
variables.why: A new action potential cannot start until the refractory period ends, so a longer refractory period lowers the ceiling on the rate.

why.correct: In cardiac muscle, calcium entering through L-type channels triggers the SR to release its calcium. With no calcium outside, there is no trigger, so the SR does not release and the ventricle stops contracting. In skeletal muscle, the voltage sensor in the T tubule opens the SR release channel directly, so outside calcium is not needed.
options: Heart muscle does have a sarcoplasmic reticulum, and it supplies most of the calcium for contraction. It just needs a calcium trigger to release it.
Correct. Cardiac SR release is calcium-induced, so it needs calcium from outside.
Skeletal muscle uses calcium from its sarcoplasmic reticulum, not from mitochondria.
The upstroke is carried by sodium, and sodium is still present in the solution. Loss of the calcium trigger, not of the upstroke, stops contraction.

why.correct: Calcium pumps in the SR membrane use ATP to move most of the calcium back into the SR. A sodium–calcium exchanger in the sarcolemma removes the smaller amount that entered from outside.
options: L-type channels let calcium into the cell, down its gradient. They cannot move it out against that gradient.
Calcium leaves troponin as cytosolic calcium falls. That is what lets the cell relax.
Calcium is an ion; it is not broken down. The main destination is the SR.
Correct. The SR pump returns most of the calcium.

why.correct: In skeletal muscle the brief action potential and its refractory period are over long before the tension peaks, so a second action potential can arrive while the fiber is still contracting and the twitches add up. In cardiac muscle the action potential lasts almost as long as the tension, so a second one cannot start until the first contraction is nearly over.
options: Correct. A short action potential inside a long twitch leaves room for another stimulus.
In both muscles the action potential comes first and triggers the rise in tension.
The graph shows the opposite: the skeletal action potential is a brief spike at the start of a much longer tension curve.
Peak tension does not decide whether twitches can sum. The timing of the refractory period relative to the contraction does.

why.correct: The upstroke is carried by sodium entering through voltage-gated sodium channels. With fewer channels available, sodium enters more slowly and the upstroke becomes slower and smaller.
options: The plateau depends mainly on calcium entering through L-type channels and potassium leaving. It is affected only indirectly.
Repolarization depends on potassium leaving through potassium channels, not on sodium channels.
The resting potential is set mainly by potassium leak channels, which the drug does not block.
Correct. Sodium channels carry phase 0, the upstroke.

why.correct: Mitochondria fill about a third of a contractile cell, and the cell makes nearly all its ATP by aerobic respiration. Without oxygen delivered by blood, ATP production falls fast, and contraction, which uses ATP, weakens.
options: Correct. Heavy dependence on aerobic respiration makes these cells vulnerable to loss of oxygen.
Heart muscle cells do not run mainly on a large glycogen store; they depend on a steady oxygen supply for aerobic respiration.
Loss of blood flow weakens the cells through lack of oxygen and ATP. Gap junctions are not what fails first.
A sudden leak of all SR calcium is not what happens when blood flow stops. The first problem is the fall in ATP production.

why.correct: In a human ventricle about three quarters of the calcium that activates contraction comes from the SR. The quarter that enters through L-type channels mainly triggers that release: calcium-induced calcium release.
options: Correct. The SR supplies most of the calcium; entering calcium triggers its release.
Outside calcium is essential. Without it there is no trigger, and the SR does not release its calcium.
Mitochondria are not a source of calcium for contraction. The two sources are the SR and the extracellular fluid.
The SR is the main source at every rate, not an extra added at fast rates. Entering calcium acts as the trigger.

why.correct: Contractile cardiac muscle cells are short, branched and striated, with one or two central nuclei, and they are joined by intercalated discs. They rest at −90 mV until charge from a neighbor brings them to threshold.
options: Yes. The cells branch, and intercalated discs join them end to end.
Yes. Each cell has one or two nuclei near its center.
Yes. Their filaments are arranged in sarcomeres, so they look striped.
No. Many peripheral nuclei describe a skeletal muscle fiber.
No. Contractile cells hold a steady resting potential and fire only when a neighbor's charge brings them to threshold.

why.correct: The SA node's pacemaker potential climbs fastest, so it reaches threshold first. Its signal then resets every slower pacemaker, so it sets the rate for the whole heart.
options: The AV node can generate a rhythm, but only about 40 to 60 per minute. The faster SA node resets it before it reaches threshold on its own.
Correct. The SA node is the heart's pacemaker because its intrinsic rate is the fastest.
Purkinje fibers have the slowest intrinsic rate, about 20 to 40 per minute. They set the rate only when no signal reaches the ventricles.
The vagus nerve slows the SA node, but it does not start beats. A heart with no nerves at all still beats.

why.correct: A steeper climb covers the same voltage distance in less time. Each cycle is shorter, so more cycles, and more beats, fit into a minute.
options: Threshold did not move, but the voltage now gets there faster. Rate depends on how long the climb takes, not only on where threshold sits.
A steeper climb shortens each cycle. Shorter cycles mean more beats per minute, not fewer.
Correct. Rate is set by how long the drift takes to reach threshold, and a steeper slope shortens it.
Nothing resets the slope while the drug is acting. As long as every climb is steeper, every cycle stays shorter.

why.correct: One full cycle, from one threshold crossing to the next, takes 0.8 seconds. 60 seconds ÷ 0.8 seconds = 75 cycles per minute.
options: 60 per minute would need a cycle of 1.0 second. The graph shows 0.8 second per cycle.
120 per minute would need a cycle of 0.5 second. That would fit two full cycles before the 1.0 second point.
40 per minute would need a cycle of 1.5 seconds. The graph shows two full cycles in 1.6 seconds.

why.correct: The voltage now has farther to climb (25 mV instead of 20 mV) and climbs more slowly, so it takes longer to reach −40 mV. Longer cycles mean fewer beats per minute. This is how parasympathetic input slows the heart.
options: Correct. A lower start and a shallower slope both lengthen the time to threshold.
The threshold is the same, but the distance to it is larger and the climb is slower. Both lengthen the cycle.
Both changes make it take longer, not shorter, to reach threshold.
Every pacemaker potential starts below threshold; that is what the slow climb is for. Starting a little lower delays firing but does not stop it.

why.correct: The SA node fires, and the signal spreads through the atria to the AV node. After the AV nodal delay it crosses the cardiac skeleton in the AV bundle, runs down the septum in the bundle branches, and spreads through the ventricular walls in the Purkinje fibers.

With no signals crossing to the ventricles, SA node signals no longer reset the ventricular conducting cells. The fastest of them, in the bundle branches or Purkinje fibers, reaches threshold on its own at about 20 to 40 per minute.
options: The SA node is still firing at 76 per minute: that is the atrial rate. Its signals cannot reach the ventricles.
The cardiac skeleton insulates the atria from the ventricles. There is no second path for atrial signals to take.
Correct. A rate of 34 fits the intrinsic rate of the bundle branches and Purkinje fibers, and it is independent of the atrial rate.
Contractile cells have a stable resting potential. They do not drift to threshold, so they cannot set a rhythm.

why.correct: Small cells pass on little current, few gap junctions let little current pass between cells, and calcium-driven upstrokes rise slowly. Together they slow conduction to about 0.05 meters per second.
options: Causes slowing. A small cell delivers little current to its neighbor, so the neighbor takes longer to reach threshold.
Causes slowing. Gap junctions carry the current from cell to cell, and the AV node has few of them.
Causes slowing. L-type calcium channels open slowly, so each cell's upstroke is slow.
Does not apply. Fast sodium channels speed conduction; Purkinje fibers have many, and they conduct fastest.
Does not apply. The AV node is only a few millimeters long. The delay comes from how slowly it conducts, not from its length.

why.correct: An SA node cell never repolarizes below about −60 mV. At that voltage its fast sodium channels stay inactivated, so the upstroke depends on L-type calcium channels, which open more slowly.
options: SA node cells have several kinds of voltage-gated channels: HCN channels, T-type and L-type calcium channels, and potassium channels.
Correct. Calcium channels open more slowly than fast sodium channels, so the upstroke is slower.
More gap junctions would speed conduction between cells; they would not slow the upstroke within a cell.
K⁺ leaves the cell when potassium channels open, which repolarizes it. It does not enter during the upstroke.

why.correct: HCN channels open when the cell becomes more negative. The inward current they carry, mostly Na⁺, is the funny current that starts the slow climb.
options: Correct. The funny current is carried by HCN channels, which open at the most negative point of the cycle.
Fast sodium channels are inactivated at SA node voltages, and they would give a sudden spike, not a slow climb.
L-type calcium channels open at threshold and carry the upstroke. They come after the slow climb, not before it.
The pump keeps running. Stopping it would slowly run down the gradients, not produce a regular drift each cycle.

why.correct: The upstroke of an SA node cell is carried by Ca²⁺ entering through L-type calcium channels. Its fast sodium channels are inactivated at its voltage.
options: This step is right. About −60 mV is the most negative point of the cycle.
This step is right. The funny current starts the pacemaker potential.
This step is right. Calcium entry through T-type channels steepens the end of the climb.
This is the error. The fast sodium upstroke belongs to contractile cells and Purkinje fibers, not SA node cells.
This step is right. Potassium exit repolarizes the cell, and the cycle starts again.

why.correct: Blocking the funny current flattens the pacemaker potential, so the SA node takes longer to reach threshold and fires less often. Drugs that do this are used to slow the heart.

variables.name: Slope of the pacemaker potential
variables.why: HCN channels carry the funny current. With less inward current, the voltage climbs more slowly.

variables.name: Time for the pacemaker potential to reach threshold
variables.why: A shallower climb covers the same distance to threshold more slowly.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Longer cycles mean fewer action potentials, and so fewer beats, per minute.

variables.name: Threshold voltage of SA node cells
variables.why: Threshold depends on the L-type calcium channels, which the drug does not touch.

why.correct: Ectopic means out of place (ec- = out of, top- = place). Any site other than the SA node that sets the heart's rhythm is an ectopic pacemaker or ectopic focus.
options: Correct. It may take over because the SA node fails, or because it fires faster than the SA node.
Heartbeats start in autorhythmic muscle cells, not nerve cells.
Cells inside the SA node are the normal pacemaker, not an out-of-place one.
A cell without gap junctions could not pass a signal on. It would not become a pacemaker for that reason.

why.correct: The SA node reaches threshold first. Its signal arrives and fires the AV node cells early, and they then start their drift again from the bottom. They are reset every beat, so they never fire on their own schedule.
options: Vagal input slows the AV node, but it does not switch off its pacemaker ability. The reason is the SA node's faster signal.
The cardiac skeleton separates atria from ventricles; the AV node is the doorway through it, not something it blocks.
AV node cells keep their pacemaker potential; each SA node signal simply cuts it short.
Correct. The fastest pacemaker resets all slower ones, so it sets the rate.

why.correct: An SA node on its own fires at about 100 per minute. In an intact heart, parasympathetic input through the vagus nerves slows it to about 70 at rest. With the nerves cut, that slowing is gone.
options: Nothing in the scenario points to extra workload, and a steady rate near 100 is exactly what an SA node with no nerve input produces.
Some hormones in blood can change heart rate, but the brain does not start heartbeats. The SA node does that by itself.
Correct. Her rate is the SA node's intrinsic rate, which vagal input normally holds down.
The AV node's intrinsic rate is about 40 to 60, well below 98.

why.correct: The signal still reaches the right ventricle through the right branch. From there it must travel muscle cell to muscle cell, through the septum and into the left ventricle, at about 0.3 to 0.5 meters per second instead of 2 to 4. The left ventricle depolarizes late and out of step.
options: Contractile cells still pass the signal to each other through gap junctions. The left ventricle is activated, only late and slowly.
The left ventricle's fast route is blocked, so it depolarizes after the right, not before.
The left Purkinje network is fed by the left branch. With that branch blocked, the signal has to arrive by the slow route through muscle, so it cannot be on time.
Correct. Losing the fast pathway forces slow muscle-to-muscle spread.

why.correct: The cardiac skeleton is connective tissue, which does not conduct action potentials. The AV bundle, leaving the AV node, is the one muscular path through it.
options: The cardiac skeleton insulates the atria from the ventricles along the whole junction, except at the AV bundle.
Correct. The AV node and AV bundle are the only normal electrical doorway.
Chordae tendineae are connective tissue cords; they do not conduct action potentials.
Bachmann's bundle carries the signal from the right atrium to the left atrium, not to the ventricles.

why.correct: Acetylcholine opens extra potassium channels, so the cell starts lower, and it reduces the funny current, so the climb is shallower. Both delay threshold and slow the heart.
options: Happens. Extra K⁺ leaving makes the inside more negative.
Happens. That is the result of the extra potassium channels being open.
Happens. Less funny current means less inward charge during the climb.
Does not happen. Norepinephrine steepens the climb; acetylcholine flattens it.
Does not happen. A lower start and a shallower climb slow the rate.

why.correct: The bundle branches run down the septum, so it depolarizes first. The network reaches the papillary muscles and apex next, then turns up the side walls, and the base near the valves is last. Contraction therefore moves from apex to base, pushing blood toward the outflow valves.
The P wave is the wave of depolarization spreading across both atria after the SA node fires.
options: Correct. The atria contract just after the P wave.
The SA node is too small for its own activity to show from the skin. The P wave comes from the much larger mass of atrial muscle.
Ventricular depolarization is the QRS complex.
Atrial repolarization happens during the QRS complex and is hidden by it.

why.correct: The atria repolarize at the same moment the ventricles depolarize. The ventricles' large signal swamps the atria's small one.
options: The atria repolarize well before the next beat; a cell must repolarize before it can fire again.
Correct. Atrial repolarization overlaps the QRS complex and is hidden in it.
Repolarization does produce a voltage change. The T wave is ventricular repolarization, for example.
The T wave is ventricular repolarization.

why.correct: The R spikes are 4 large squares apart. 4 × 0.20 second = 0.80 second per beat, and 60 ÷ 0.80 = 75 beats per minute. The shortcut gives the same: 300 ÷ 4 = 75.
options: 60 per minute would need 5 large squares (1.0 second) between beats.
100 per minute would need 3 large squares (0.60 second) between beats.
Correct. The R spikes are 4 large squares apart, and 300 ÷ 4 = 75.
This uses 0.04 second, the width of a small square, for each large square: 4 × 0.04 = 0.16 second, and 60 ÷ 0.16 = 375.

why.correct: The PR interval runs from the start of atrial depolarization to the start of ventricular depolarization. Most of that time is the AV nodal delay, so slower AV conduction lengthens it.
options: The QRS complex measures how fast the ventricles depolarize, after the signal has left the AV node.
The ST segment is the plateau after the ventricles have depolarized. The AV node plays no part.
The QT interval covers ventricular depolarization and repolarization, which start after the AV node.
Correct. The PR interval is the window on the AV node.

why.correct: Beats per minute = 60 seconds ÷ seconds per beat = 60 ÷ 0.60 = 100. The shortcut 300 ÷ 3 gives the same.
options: Multiplying gives 36, which has no meaning here. Divide a minute by the time per beat.
The shortcut divides 300 by the number of squares; it does not multiply. 300 × 3 = 900.
This gives 0.01, the number of minutes per beat, not beats per minute.

why.correct: A PR interval longer than 0.20 second means the AV node conducts slowly. Because every P wave still reaches the ventricles, it is first-degree heart block.
options: In third-degree block no signals cross, so P waves and QRS complexes are unrelated. Here every P wave is followed by its QRS.
Atrial fibrillation has no P waves and an irregular rhythm. This rhythm is regular with a P wave before every beat.
Correct. Every beat conducts, but each is delayed at the AV node.
Ventricular tachycardia is fast, with wide QRS complexes and no linked P waves.

why.correct: This is atrial fibrillation. Chaotic atrial wavelets replace the P wave, and the AV node lets signals through at irregular times, giving irregularly irregular narrow QRS complexes.
options: Correct. Narrow QRS complexes show the ventricles are still activated through the normal conducting system.
Sinus tachycardia would be regular, with a P wave before each QRS complex.
In ventricular fibrillation there are no QRS complexes at all. Hers are clear and narrow.
A ventricular backup pacemaker would give a slow, regular rhythm with wide QRS complexes.

why.correct: This is ventricular fibrillation. A shock depolarizes most of the heart at once, so all those cells become refractory together, the chaotic wavelets die out, and the SA node can take back control.
options: A pacemaker adds regular pulses to a heart that is too slow. It cannot stop chaotic activity already running through the ventricles.
The problem is in the ventricles, not the AV node. Slowing the AV node would not reach the chaotic ventricular wavelets.
Correct. Defibrillation resets the ventricles' chaotic electrical activity.
Ventricular fibrillation pumps no blood. It rarely stops on its own, and death follows within minutes without a shock.

why.correct: A beat that starts in ventricular muscle spreads slowly from cell to cell instead of through the Purkinje network, so its QRS complex is wide and oddly shaped, and it has no P wave in front of it.
options: Expected. Slow muscle-to-muscle spread makes the QRS complex wide.
Expected. The atria did not start this beat, so no P wave leads into it.
Not expected. A normal PR interval means the beat came from the atria through the AV node.
Not expected. Without the fast conducting network, depolarization takes longer, not shorter.
Expected. The unusual path of spread changes the direction the lead sees, and so the shape.

why.correct: The atria depolarize (P wave), the signal crosses the AV node (PR segment), the ventricles depolarize (QRS complex), they hold their plateau (ST segment), and they repolarize (T wave).

During the ST segment the ventricles are fully depolarized, sitting in the plateau of their action potential. With every cell at about the same voltage, little current flows between regions, so the line is flat.
options: This statement is right.
This statement is right. The PR interval spans the atria, the AV node and the conducting fibers, and the AV node takes most of the time.
This statement is right.
This is the error. The ventricles are fully depolarized, not repolarized, during the ST segment. They repolarize during the T wave.
This statement is right.

why.correct: Slowing the AV node stretches the gap between each P wave and its QRS complex without changing the rate of P waves or the width of the QRS.

variables.name: PR interval
variables.why: The PR interval is mostly AV nodal delay, so slower AV conduction lengthens it.

variables.name: Number of P waves per minute
variables.why: The SA node sets how often P waves occur, and the drug does not affect it.

variables.name: QRS duration
variables.why: Once the signal leaves the AV node, the ventricles depolarize through the normal fast network, at the normal speed.

why.correct: Normally all ventricular cells sit at the same plateau voltage during the ST segment, so no current flows and the line is flat. Ischemic cells cannot hold that voltage, so a voltage difference appears between them and healthy cells, and the segment shifts off the baseline.
options: Faster depolarization would change the QRS complex, and injured cells tend to conduct more slowly, not faster.
Correct. The ST segment is normally silent; injury makes current flow during it.
Loss of AV conduction affects the P-to-QRS relationship, not the level of the ST segment.
Each ventricular cell repolarizes once per beat, during the T wave.

why.correct: Defibrillation depolarizes the heart all at once, so every cell becomes refractory together and chaotic wavelets die out. With no electrical activity at all, there is nothing for the shock to reset, and it cannot start a beat.
options: Shocks are the standard treatment for ventricular fibrillation, a ventricular rhythm.
A shock does not speed up the heart; it resets its electrical activity once.
A firing SA node would produce P waves. A flat line means no electrical activity is reaching the skin, which is an emergency.
Correct. A flat line needs chest compressions and drugs, not a shock.

why.correct: Depolarization moving toward a positive electrode draws an upward deflection; moving away from it draws a downward one.
options: Correct. Movement away from the positive electrode points the trace down.
An upward deflection means depolarization is moving toward the positive electrode.
A small or flat deflection means the wave is moving at right angles to the lead.
A two-part deflection of equal size fits a wave passing across the lead, not one heading directly away.

why.correct: A 6-second strip is one tenth of a minute, so multiply by 10: 11 × 10 = 110 per minute. This method works when the spacing between beats varies.
options: This multiplies by 6 instead of 10. There are ten 6-second periods in a minute.
This halves the correct answer, as if the strip were 12 seconds long.
This would need 18 complexes in 6 seconds.

why.correct: P waves and QRS complexes marching independently mean no signals cross from atria to ventricles: third-degree block. A rate of 36 with wide complexes fits a backup pacemaker in the bundle branches or Purkinje fibers, whose intrinsic rate is 20 to 40.
options: The SA node is pacing the atria at 80. Its signals are not reaching the ventricles.
An AV node pacemaker would usually give 40 to 60 per minute with narrow QRS complexes, because its signal would still use the bundle branches and Purkinje fibers.
Atrial signals are not reaching the ventricles at all, so the atria cannot be pacing them.
Correct. The slow rate and wide QRS complexes both point to a pacemaker below the AV bundle.

why.correct: The QT interval spans ventricular depolarization and repolarization, so it tracks how long the ventricular action potential lasts. A long QT means the cells take longer to repolarize.
options: Slow depolarization would widen the QRS complex. A long QT with a normal QRS points to slow repolarization.
Late arrival from the atria lengthens the PR interval, which is measured before the QT interval starts.
Correct. Drugs, inherited channel disorders and low blood potassium can all lengthen the action potential.
A problem with the Purkinje network would change the QRS complex, not mainly the time to repolarize.

why.correct: An ECG records only electrical events. Normally contraction follows each one, but electrical activity can continue even when the muscle fails to pump, for example after severe blood loss or when fluid compresses the heart. The patient needs treatment for that cause, not a shock.
options: Monitors display in real time. The mismatch is real, not a display delay.
Correct. Electrical activity and pumping are separate events, and the ECG shows only the first.
The QRS complexes show the ventricles are depolarizing; the problem is that the muscle is not pumping effectively after that.
An ECG cannot show pumping. A normal-looking rhythm with no pulse is a recognized emergency.

why.correct: Valves open and close only because of the pressure difference across them. When pressure behind the aortic valve (in the ventricle) exceeds pressure in front of it (in the aorta), blood pushes the cusps aside.
options: Papillary muscles attach to the atrioventricular valves, not the semilunar valves, and they never pull any valve open.
Correct. The valve opens when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, at about 80 mm Hg at rest.
Valves have no muscle and receive no nerve signals. The QRS complex triggers ventricular contraction, which raises pressure; pressure then opens the valve.
Higher pressure in the aorta than in the ventricle pushes blood backward into the cusps, which closes the valve.

why.correct: Ventricular pressure has risen above atrial pressure, which closed the mitral valve, but it is still below aortic pressure, so the aortic valve stays shut. With both closed, volume cannot change while pressure climbs.
options: The mitral valve closed at the very start of this phase, when ventricular pressure rose above atrial pressure.
The aortic valve opens only when ventricular pressure passes aortic pressure, which ends this phase.
Both valves open at once would let blood flow straight from atrium to aorta. That never happens in a normal heart.
Correct. That is what isovolumetric means: the volume stays the same because blood cannot leave or enter.

why.correct: The aortic valve opens where the rising ventricular trace crosses the aortic trace. Aortic pressure has fallen to its lowest value, about 80 mm Hg, so that is where the crossing happens.
options: A few mm Hg, near the bottom of the graph, is where the mitral valve closes, as ventricular pressure first rises above atrial pressure.
120 mm Hg is the peak reached during ejection, after the valve is already open.
Correct. Ventricular pressure must exceed aortic pressure, about 80 mm Hg, before the valve opens.
About 100 mm Hg is near where the aortic valve closes at the end of ejection, not where it opens.

why.correct: Between those two events ventricular pressure is above atrial pressure (mitral valve shut) and below aortic pressure (aortic valve shut). Blood can neither enter nor leave, so volume is constant while pressure climbs: isovolumetric contraction.
options: The mitral valve has closed, so no more blood can enter from the atrium.
Correct. Both valves are closed, so blood can neither enter nor leave: isovolumetric contraction.
Ejection starts only once the aortic valve opens, at the end of this interval.
A healthy closed mitral valve does not leak, and the aortic valve is still shut, so no blood leaves.

why.correct: The QRS complex is ventricular depolarization, which triggers ventricular contraction. On the chart, ventricular systole begins at the QRS complex.
options: The P wave is atrial depolarization. It leads to atrial systole, not ventricular systole.
Correct. Electrical depolarization comes just before the contraction it triggers.
The T wave is ventricular repolarization. Ventricular systole ends around the end of the T wave.
After the T wave the ventricles are relaxed and filling: ventricular diastole.

why.correct: The atria top off the ventricles; the ventricles contract with both valves closed until the aortic valve opens; blood is ejected; the aortic valve closes and pressure falls with both valves closed; the mitral valve opens and the ventricles fill until the atria contract again.
Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume: 70 ÷ 130 = 0.54, which is 54 percent.
options: This divides the volume left behind (ESV) by EDV, giving the fraction that stays, 46 percent.
This divides by ESV instead of EDV, giving 117 percent, which is impossible for a fraction ejected.
Correct. EF = SV ÷ EDV × 100.
This inverts the fraction and gives 186 percent.

why.correct: EF = SV ÷ EDV × 100 = 60 ÷ 150 × 100 = 40 percent. That is clearly below the normal range of about 50 to 70 percent.
options: This is the fraction left behind: ESV = 150 − 60 = 90 mL, and 90 ÷ 150 = 60 percent.
This is the ESV in mL (150 − 60 = 90), not a percentage ejected.
This divides 60 by 240, which has no meaning here.

why.correct: A: SV = 70 mL, EF = 70 ÷ 120 = 58 percent. B: SV = 65 mL, EF = 65 ÷ 200 = 33 percent. The stroke volumes are close, but B's enlarged ventricle ejects only a third of its contents. Ejection fraction reveals the weakness that stroke volume hides.
options: Correct. 70 versus 65 mL per beat, but 58 versus 33 percent ejected.
B pumps slightly less per beat (65 versus 70 mL), and its low ejection fraction points to a weaker ventricle.
A ejects 58 percent and B ejects 33 percent.
A has the higher ejection fraction (58 versus 33 percent) and the larger stroke volume (70 versus 65 mL).

why.correct: The murmur falls between S1 and S2, so it happens during ventricular systole. A narrowed (stenotic) aortic valve makes blood jet through a small opening during ejection, and the turbulence is heard as a murmur, best at the aortic listening spot.
options: Backflow through a leaky aortic valve happens in diastole, after S2, not between S1 and S2.
Correct. This is aortic stenosis.
A leaky mitral valve also gives a murmur during systole, but it is heard best at the apex, and his ultrasound shows the aortic valve is the problem.
Early filling happens in diastole, after S2. Normal filling is usually silent.

why.correct: A narrowed outflow valve makes the ventricle work at higher pressure, creates a large pressure gradient and turbulence across the valve, and, when severe, reduces how much is ejected. Over time the left ventricular wall thickens.

variables.name: Peak left ventricular pressure
variables.why: The narrowed opening resists flow, so the ventricle must generate a higher pressure to drive blood through it.

variables.name: Pressure difference between left ventricle and aorta
variables.why: Normally the two pressures run almost together during ejection. Across a narrow valve, a large difference is needed to push blood through.

variables.name: Turbulence of flow through the aortic valve
variables.why: Blood jets through the small opening at high speed and swirls, which is heard as a murmur between S1 and S2.

variables.name: Stroke volume
variables.why: Less blood gets through the narrowed valve in the time available, so more is left behind: ESV rises and SV = EDV − ESV falls.

why.correct: The aortic valve has just closed (S2) and the mitral valve has not yet opened, so the relaxing ventricle loses pressure with no change in volume, which stays at ESV.
options: True. Aortic pressure is above ventricular pressure, and ventricular pressure is still above atrial pressure.
True. The muscle is relaxing inside a sealed chamber.
True. No blood can enter or leave until the mitral valve opens.
False. The aortic valve closed at the start of this phase, so ejection has ended.
False. The mitral valve opens only when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, which ends this phase.

why.correct: Closure of the semilunar valves, including the aortic valve, makes the second heart sound, S2 (dub). S1 (lub) comes from atrioventricular valve closure.
options: This statement is right. It starts isovolumetric contraction.
This statement is right. S1 is atrioventricular valve closure.
This statement is right. It starts ejection.
This is the error. Aortic valve closure is S2, which marks the end of ventricular systole.
This statement is right. It ends isovolumetric relaxation and starts filling.

why.correct: As the ventricle relaxes, its pressure drops below aortic pressure. Blood in the aorta briefly flows back toward the ventricle and fills the valve cusps, which snap shut. The sudden stop against the closed valve gives a small dip and rebound in aortic pressure.
options: The atria empty into the ventricles, not the aorta, and they contract near the end of diastole, not when the notch appears.
Papillary muscles act on the atrioventricular valves. They play no part at the aortic valve.
The ventricle contracts once per beat. The notch comes from the valve closing, not from a second squeeze.
Correct. The notch marks aortic valve closure and the end of ejection.

why.correct: When the atrioventricular valves close, the moving blood behind them is halted suddenly. That abrupt stop sets the blood, the valve structures and the chamber walls vibrating together, and the stethoscope picks up the vibration.
options: Muscle contraction itself is essentially silent through a stethoscope. The sound is timed to valve closure.
The cusps are too thin and soft to make an audible clap. The sound comes from the vibration of the whole blood-filled system.
Correct. The heart sounds are vibrations set up by blood decelerating against closing valves.
Outflow through normal semilunar valves is smooth and silent, and it happens after S1, not at it.

why.correct: The right edge of the loop is EDV and the left edge is ESV, so the width is the stroke volume: 140 − 60 = 80 mL.
options: 60 mL is the left edge, the ESV: the volume left behind.
140 mL is the right edge, the EDV: the volume before contraction.
Adding the two volumes has no meaning. Stroke volume is their difference.
Correct. SV = EDV − ESV = 140 − 60.

why.correct: A vertical line means pressure changes with no change in volume. At the largest volume (EDV), with pressure rising, that is isovolumetric contraction, between mitral valve closure and aortic valve opening.
options: During filling, volume rises, so the line runs across the bottom of the loop, not up the side.
During ejection volume falls, so that side runs across the top from right to left.
Correct. Rising pressure at constant maximum volume is isovolumetric contraction.
Isovolumetric relaxation is also vertical, but pressure falls and it sits at the smallest volume (ESV), on the left side.

why.correct: Blood leaks backward through a valve whenever the pressure gradient drives it the wrong way while the valve should be shut. For the mitral valve that is all of ventricular systole, when left ventricular pressure (up to about 120 mm Hg) far exceeds atrial pressure. The leak makes a murmur between S1 and S2.
options: During filling the mitral valve is supposed to be open, and blood flows forward, from atrium to ventricle, down its pressure gradient.
Correct. Left ventricular pressure is far above atrial pressure throughout systole, so blood is driven backward through the leaky valve: mitral regurgitation, a murmur between S1 and S2.
Atrial contraction pushes blood forward into the ventricle through the open mitral valve.

Leaking starts as soon as ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure, so it runs through isovolumetric contraction and ejection. By the end of relaxation, ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure and the backward push stops.

why.correct: At 75 per minute each cycle lasts 0.8 second, with about 0.3 second of ventricular systole and 0.5 of diastole. At 150 per minute the cycle is 0.4 second; systole shrinks only a little, to about 0.25 second, so diastole drops to about 0.15 second.
options: Ejection shortens only slightly as the rate rises.
Isovolumetric contraction is already very short, about 0.05 second, and changes little.
Atrial contraction lasts about 0.1 second and changes little.
Correct. Nearly all the lost time comes out of diastole, the ventricles' time to relax and fill.

why.correct: End-diastolic volume (EDV) is the volume at the end of ventricular diastole, just before systole. At rest it is about 120 mL.
options: That is stroke volume, EDV − ESV.
Correct. It is the largest volume of the cycle.
That is end-systolic volume (ESV), about 50 mL at rest.
The atrial contribution is only part of the filling, about 20 percent at rest.

why.correct: SV = EDV − ESV. Stroke volume rises if the ventricle starts fuller (higher EDV) or empties further (lower ESV).
options: Increases SV. Starting with more blood and leaving the same amount means more is ejected.
Increases SV. Leaving less blood behind from the same starting volume means more is ejected.
Decreases SV. More is left behind from the same starting volume.
Decreases SV. Less is available to eject while the same amount stays behind.
No change. The difference between the two stays the same.

why.correct: The tunica media is the middle layer: rings of smooth muscle mixed with elastic fibers. Its contraction narrows the vessel.
options: The tunica intima is the endothelial lining with a thin layer of connective tissue. It has no muscle layer.
The tunica externa is mostly collagen. It anchors the vessel and resists overstretching.
Correct. The media is the muscle layer.
The basement membrane is the thin sheet the endothelium sits on, part of the tunica intima.

why.correct: A capillary wall is only the tunica intima: one layer of endothelial cells and its basement membrane. That keeps the diffusion distance between blood and tissue tiny.
options: Capillaries have no tunica media and no tunica externa.
Correct. Pericytes wrap around some capillaries, but the wall itself is one cell thick.
Capillaries have no smooth muscle layer. Arterioles do.
Every vessel is lined by endothelium; capillaries have nothing else.

why.correct: The elastic artery's tunica media is packed with layers of elastic fibers. They stretch as blood surges in during ejection and recoil when the aortic valve closes, pushing blood onward during diastole.
options: The arteriole's wall is mostly a few smooth muscle cells. It adjusts resistance rather than storing stretch.
The muscular artery's media is mostly smooth muscle with fewer elastic fibers, so it stretches much less.
The walls differ in elastic content, and so in how much they stretch and recoil.
Correct. Elastic arteries, such as the aorta, act as the pressure reservoir between beats.

why.correct: Sinusoids have large gaps between endothelial cells and an incomplete basement membrane, so large proteins and even blood cells can pass. The liver, spleen and red bone marrow have them.
options: Correct. The gaps between cells and the incomplete basement membrane let large proteins through.
Continuous capillaries let small solutes through their clefts, but their unbroken wall and complete basement membrane hold back large proteins.
Fenestrated capillaries pass fluid and small molecules quickly through their pores, but their complete basement membrane holds back most large proteins.
The liver is full of capillaries; they are the sinusoid type.

why.correct: Squeezing raises pressure in that segment. Blood tries to flow both ways, but downward flow fills the cusps of the lower valve and shuts it, so blood can only move up through the valve above.
options: Backward flow is exactly what closes a venous valve. Blood cannot pass down through it.
Correct. Like heart valves, venous valves close when pressure in front of them exceeds pressure behind them: here, pressure in the squeezed segment is higher than below it.
The lower valve closes during contraction; the upper valve closes during relaxation.
The valve closes because of a pressure difference, not because muscle touches it.

why.correct: Thick walls are too far from the lumen for diffusion to feed them. The vasa vasorum, small vessels in the tunica externa, supply the outer layers.
options: The nerves in the wall are the nervi vasorum, and capillaries have no smooth muscle for them to control.
Correct. The name means vessels of the vessels.
That is an arteriovenous anastomosis.
Venous valves are folds of the tunica intima.

why.correct: Resistance depends on 1 ÷ radius to the fourth power, so small vessels resist flow strongly and small changes in their radius matter a great deal. Arterioles also have the most smooth muscle relative to their size, so they can change radius widely.
options: Pressure is highest in the large arteries; it drops as blood passes through the arterioles.
Large arteries have thicker walls. Arterioles have thick walls only relative to their small lumen.
Correct. Small radius plus strong control of radius makes arterioles the resistance vessels.
Every vessel, arterioles included, is lined by endothelium.

why.correct: More sympathetic tone narrows the skin's arterioles, raising their resistance and cutting flow into the skin, which reduces heat loss from warm blood near the surface.

variables.name: Arteriole radius
variables.why: Norepinephrine binds alpha adrenergic receptor proteins on the smooth muscle, which contracts further and narrows the vessel.

variables.name: Arteriole resistance
variables.why: Resistance depends on 1 ÷ radius to the fourth power, so a smaller radius raises it steeply.

variables.name: Blood flow into the skin's capillary beds
variables.why: With the pressure gradient about the same and resistance higher, flow = ΔP ÷ R falls.

why.correct: Fenestrated capillaries have pores through their endothelial cells that let fluid and small molecules, such as many hormones, pass quickly. Endocrine glands, the kidneys and the intestinal lining have them.
options: Tight-junction-sealed continuous capillaries, as in the brain, restrict passage. That fits a barrier, not a gland that releases hormones.
Correct. Pores speed exchange of small molecules.
Anastomoses shunt blood past the capillary bed, so less exchange would happen, not more.
Exchange with tissues happens in capillaries; veins are too thick-walled.

why.correct: One incompetent valve lets blood fall back and pool. The pooled blood raises pressure and stretches the thin wall, and the widening pulls the next valve's cusps apart. The failure spreads, and the veins become swollen and twisted.
Veins carry blood at low pressure, and their walls reflect it: a thin media, a relatively thick externa, and a wide lumen that collapses when empty.
options: Identifies the vein. Low pressure needs little muscle.
Identifies the vein. Its thickest layer is the collagen-rich externa.
Identifies the vein. The thin wall collapses without blood pressure holding it open.
Identifies the artery. The internal elastic membrane is prominent in arteries.
Identifies the artery. A thick muscular media keeps the artery round even when empty.

why.correct: About 60 to 65 percent of blood sits in the compliant systemic veins. Sympathetic venoconstriction reduces their capacity, raises venous pressure and pushes that stored blood toward the heart, partly making up for the volume lost.
options: Dilating the veins would let more blood pool in them, which is the opposite of what she needs.
Valves are passive. Nerves do not open or close them, and blocking flow would stop venous return.
Correct. The veins act as a blood reservoir the body can draw on.
Capillary type is a fixed structural feature of each tissue; nerves do not change it within minutes.

why.correct: Lower pressure around the veins in the chest and higher pressure around those in the abdomen widen the pressure gradient toward the heart, so venous return rises. This is the respiratory pump.
options: Correct. A wider pressure gradient increases flow.
Flow slows when you breathe out, when the pressure changes reverse.
Flow toward the heart continues through both phases of breathing; it only speeds up and slows down.
Venous valves in the limbs and the direction of the gradient keep flow heading toward the heart.

why.correct: When the muscle relaxes, pressure in the segment falls. Blood above starts to flow back, fills the cusps of the valve above and closes it, so blood cannot fall back. The segment refills from below.
options: This step is right. Many limb veins run between and through skeletal muscles.
This step is right. Squeezing a closed segment raises its pressure.
This step is right. Higher pressure in the squeezed segment pushes the valve above open and the valve below shut.
This step is right. The closed lower valve leaves only one way out.
This is the error. The valve above closes on relaxation; that is what stops blood from falling back.

why.correct: Standing still switches off the skeletal muscle pump. Blood pools in the compliant leg veins under gravity, less blood returns to the heart, less is pumped out, and blood flow to the brain falls until he faints. Heat widens skin vessels and adds to the pooling.
options: Arteries do not stiffen in an hour, and higher pressure to the brain would not cause fainting.
Correct. Venous return depends on the muscle pump when you are upright.
Valves do not fail suddenly; varicose veins develop over years.
His heart rate may rise, but the problem starts with too little blood returning, not with the heart.

why.correct: Arteriolar smooth muscle sets the resistance at the entrance to each bed and responds to nerves and to local chemicals. Discrete precapillary sphincters have been found in only some tissues and species, and their role in humans is unsettled. For your exam, many tests still expect the answer "precapillary sphincters".
options: Correct. Arterioles are the resistance vessels that set flow into each bed.
Venous valves only stop backflow in veins. They do not control flow into capillaries.
Venule pericytes support the wall and affect its leakiness; they do not meter flow into the bed.
Pores affect what crosses the wall, not how much blood flows through the bed.

why.correct: A stiffer aorta works less well as an elastic reservoir: pressure rises higher during each ejection and falls lower between beats.

variables.name: How much the aorta stretches during ejection
variables.why: Collagen resists stretch far more than elastic fibers, so the wall gives less.

variables.name: Peak aortic pressure during ejection
variables.why: The same volume forced into a less stretchy tube raises its pressure more.

variables.name: Lowest aortic pressure between beats
variables.why: Less stretch stored means less recoil during diastole to keep pressure up.

why.correct: An arteriovenous anastomosis links an arteriole straight to a venule, so blood can skip the capillary bed. It is one kind of vascular shunt, common in the skin of the fingers, toes and ears.
options: Those are the vasa vasorum.
That is a fenestration.
Correct. Anastomosis means a connection between vessels.
That describes a venous valve.

why.correct: Veins are highly compliant: their thin walls stretch with little rise in pressure. That is why they can hold most of the blood volume as a reservoir. The thick artery wall resists stretch, so the same volume raises its pressure far more.
options: A stronger, stiffer wall stretches less, so the same added volume raises the artery's pressure more, not less.
Their compliances differ greatly, so their pressures change by different amounts.
Adding volume to a closed elastic tube always raises its pressure.
Correct. This is what makes veins capacitance vessels.

why.correct: (½)⁴ = ½ × ½ × ½ × ½ = 1/16. Resistance depends on 1 ÷ radius to the fourth power, so it becomes 16 times as large.
options: That is the radius itself, not the radius to the fourth power.
That is (½)³, the cube, not the fourth power.
Correct. (½)⁴ = 1/16.
Halving the radius makes the fourth-power term smaller, not larger.

why.correct: The brachiocephalic trunk (brachi- = arm, cephal- = head) is the first and largest branch of the aortic arch. It exists only on the right and splits into the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries.
options: The right common carotid artery is one of the two branches the pinned vessel splits into. It runs up the neck from the end of the trunk.
Correct. The brachiocephalic trunk serves both the right arm and the right side of the head, which is what its name says.
The right subclavian artery is the other branch the pinned vessel splits into. It heads out under the clavicle toward the arm.
The ascending aorta is the part of the aorta below the arch. Its only branches are the coronary arteries.

why.correct: The celiac trunk leaves the front of the aorta at about T12, just below the aortic hiatus. It splits at once into the left gastric artery, the splenic artery and the common hepatic artery.
options: The superior mesenteric artery is the second single gut branch, leaving the aorta at about L1, a little below the pinned vessel.
The renal arteries are paired and leave the sides of the aorta, not the front. The pinned artery is single.
Correct. The celiac trunk is the highest of the three single gut arteries.
The inferior mesenteric artery is the lowest single gut branch, at about L3, not the first one below the diaphragm.

why.correct: The two vertebral arteries join in the midline to form the basilar artery (basi- = base). At its top it splits into the two posterior cerebral arteries.
options: The anterior communicating artery is also a single midline vessel, but it sits at the front of the ring and joins the two anterior cerebral arteries.
The internal carotid arteries are paired and enter the ring at its sides, not in the midline on the brainstem.
The posterior cerebral arteries are paired. They are the branches the pinned artery splits into at its top end.
Correct. The basilar artery is formed by the two vertebral arteries.

why.correct: The left subclavian artery is the third branch of the aortic arch. Unlike the right subclavian, it comes straight off the arch.
options: Correct. The left subclavian artery arises directly from the arch and runs under the left clavicle.
The left common carotid artery is the middle branch of the arch, and it runs up the neck, not toward the arm.
The brachiocephalic trunk is the first branch, on the right. There is no left brachiocephalic trunk.
The axillary artery is the same vessel further out, after it crosses the first rib into the armpit. It does not leave the arch.

why.correct: The dorsalis pedis artery (dorsum = top, ped- = foot) is the continuation of the anterior tibial artery onto the top of the foot, where it lies over the tarsal bones.
options: The posterior tibial pulse is felt behind the bump on the inner ankle, not on the top of the foot.
The popliteal pulse is felt deep behind the knee.
The femoral pulse is felt in the groin.
Correct. The dorsalis pedis pulse is on the top of the foot.

why.correct: From the aortic arch, the right arm is served through the brachiocephalic trunk, which gives the right subclavian artery. That one tube is renamed axillary at the outer edge of the first rib and brachial below the armpit, then splits in front of the elbow into the radial and ulnar arteries. The radial artery carries the wrist pulse.
The femoral artery passes to the back of the knee and is renamed the popliteal artery. Below the knee, the popliteal artery splits into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
options: The deep femoral artery is a side branch of the femoral artery that supplies the thigh muscles. It does not continue to the leg below the knee.
Correct. The popliteal artery links the femoral artery to the tibial arteries.
The internal iliac artery branches off before the femoral artery exists, and it supplies the pelvis.
The dorsalis pedis artery comes after the anterior tibial artery, on the top of the foot. It is not between the femoral and tibial arteries.

why.correct: Blood bound for the leg goes from the common iliac into the external iliac artery, which passes under the inguinal ligament to become the femoral artery. The internal iliac artery dives into the pelvis and supplies the pelvic organs and buttocks.
options: This step is right. The left ventricle ejects into the ascending aorta through the aortic valve.
This step is right. The arch continues as the descending aorta, whose chest part is the thoracic aorta.
This step is right. The abdominal aorta ends at about L4 by splitting into the right and left common iliac arteries.
This is the error. The route to the leg uses the external iliac artery, not the internal iliac artery.
This step is right. The femoral artery is renamed popliteal behind the knee.
This step is right. The anterior tibial artery becomes the dorsalis pedis artery at the ankle.

why.correct: The three gut arteries (celiac trunk, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric) leave the front of the aorta singly. Arteries to the kidneys, gonads and legs are paired, one on each side.
options: Correct. The celiac trunk is single and supplies the stomach, liver, spleen and part of the pancreas.
The renal arteries are paired, one to each kidney.
Correct. The superior mesenteric artery is single and supplies the small bowel and first half of the large bowel.
The gonadal arteries are paired, one to each testis or ovary.
Correct. The inferior mesenteric artery is single and supplies the second half of the large bowel.
The common iliac arteries are paired: the aorta ends by splitting into a right and a left one.

why.correct: In an unresponsive adult, check the carotid pulse. The carotid is a large artery close to the heart, so a pulse can often still be felt there when pressure is too low to push a wave out to the wrist or foot.
options: The radial pulse is the routine pulse in a responsive patient. When pressure is low it can disappear while the heart is still pumping, so its absence does not settle the question.
The dorsalis pedis pulse is the farthest from the heart and the first to fade when pressure falls. It is used to check blood flow to the foot.
Correct. The carotid pulse is the standard check in an unresponsive adult.
The brachial pulse is the standard check in an infant, whose short neck makes the carotid hard to find. In an adult the carotid is preferred.

why.correct: The cerebral arterial circle is an anastomosis. Blood from the right internal carotid can cross through the anterior communicating artery, and blood from the basilar artery can come forward through the left posterior communicating artery, into the left anterior and middle cerebral arteries. Slow narrowing gives these small connections time to enlarge.
options: The vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery, which serves the back of the brain. They reach the front of the left cerebrum only by way of the circle, so the circle is the real explanation.
Correct. The circle gives blood a second route around a blocked internal carotid artery.
The external carotid artery supplies the face and scalp, outside the skull. It does not normally supply the cerebrum.
The carotid sinus is a pressure sensor at the start of the internal carotid. It does not create a new route for blood past a block.

why.correct: The aorta passes through the diaphragm at the aortic hiatus, at about T12. Above it, the descending aorta is the thoracic aorta; below it, the abdominal aorta.
options: The top of the arch is where the three large branches to the head and arms leave. The thoracic aorta begins only after the arch ends, at about T4.
Correct. The diaphragm divides the chest from the abdomen, and the aortic hiatus is where the aorta crosses it.
The renal arteries leave the abdominal aorta at about L1–L2, well below where it begins.
The split into the common iliac arteries, at about L4, is where the abdominal aorta ends, not where it begins.

why.correct: The superior mesenteric artery is a separate single branch of the aorta, leaving about 1 cm below the celiac trunk. The celiac trunk's three branches go to the stomach, spleen and liver.
options: The left gastric artery is a celiac branch. It supplies the stomach.
The splenic artery is a celiac branch. It runs to the spleen and gives branches to the pancreas and stomach.
Correct. The superior mesenteric artery arises from the aorta itself, not from the celiac trunk.
The common hepatic branch is a celiac branch. It gives an artery to the stomach and bowel and then continues to the liver.

why.correct: Behind the medial malleolus is the posterior tibial pulse; on the top of the foot is the dorsalis pedis pulse, the continuation of the anterior tibial artery. A pulse missing on the injured side only points to an artery squeezed or torn by the injury or the splint.
options: Correct. Distal pulses show whether blood is getting past the injury to the foot.
The femoral pulse is felt in the groin, above the injury. Pressing at the ankle and foot cannot tell you about it, and it could not show whether blood gets past a break lower down.
Heart rate is counted at the wrist or neck. Comparing the two feet side by side is about flow to each foot, not about the rate.
Pressing on pulse points tests arteries, not nerves. Sensation is checked separately, by touching the skin and asking what the patient feels.

why.correct: You can feel a pulse only where an artery lies near the skin over something firm. The vertebral arteries climb through the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae, so bone surrounds them and your fingers cannot press them.
options: The pulse is a pressure wave in the artery wall, not the blood's own speed. The vertebral arteries carry a pulse wave like every systemic artery.
Correct. They lie deep in the neck, inside a column of bone, so your fingers cannot press them against anything.
Arteries of this size have elastic tissue in their walls, and the pulse wave travels along them. The reason is where they run.
Every systemic artery receives blood through the whole cardiac cycle, and the vertebral arteries are no exception.

why.correct: The ejected blood stretches the aorta's elastic wall, and that bulge travels down the arteries as a pressure wave. The wave moves several meters per second, far faster than the blood itself, which takes much longer to reach the hand.
options: The blood from that beat moves much more slowly than the wave. It is still in the large arteries near the heart when the pulse is felt at the wrist.
No nerve runs from the heart to the wrist to make a pulse. The pulse is a mechanical wave.
Correct. The pulse is a pressure wave in the artery wall.
Blood does not flow backward from the capillaries. The pulse comes from the heart's side of the circulation.

why.correct: The brachial artery runs down the inner side of the arm beside the humerus and splits in front of the elbow into the radial artery (thumb side) and the ulnar artery (little-finger side).
options: The axillary artery is the same tube higher up, in the armpit. It becomes the brachial artery before reaching the elbow.
The subclavian artery is the same tube where it crosses the first rib, far above the elbow.
Correct. The brachial artery ends by splitting into the two forearm arteries.
The palmar arches are in the hand. They are formed where the radial and ulnar arteries join, not where they begin.

why.correct: The circle is built from the anterior communicating artery, the two anterior cerebral arteries, the ends of the two internal carotid arteries, the two posterior communicating arteries and the two posterior cerebral arteries from the basilar artery.
options: Correct. It joins the two anterior cerebral arteries at the front of the ring.
The external carotid artery stays outside the skull and supplies the face and scalp.
Correct. Each one joins an internal carotid artery to a posterior cerebral artery.
Correct. Each internal carotid artery feeds the ring and ends there as the anterior and middle cerebral arteries.
The facial artery is a branch of the external carotid artery on the face, far from the brain.

why.correct: The median cubital vein (cubit- = elbow) crosses the front of the elbow diagonally between the cephalic and basilic veins. It is the usual site for drawing blood.
options: The cephalic vein runs up the thumb side of the forearm and the outer arm. It is one of the two veins the pinned vein connects.
Correct. The median cubital vein links the cephalic and basilic veins in front of the elbow.
The basilic vein runs up the little-finger side and the inner arm. It is the other vein the pinned vein connects.
The brachial veins are deep veins that run beside the brachial artery. They are not visible under the skin.

why.correct: The great saphenous vein starts at the inner end of the dorsal venous arch and joins the femoral vein just below the groin. It is the longest vein in the body.
options: The femoral vein is a deep vein that runs beside the femoral artery. The great saphenous vein drains into it at the groin.
The small saphenous vein runs up the back of the calf from behind the outer ankle and ends at the knee.
The popliteal vein is a deep vein behind the knee. It does not run up the inner side of the thigh.
Correct. The great saphenous vein runs the length of the inner leg.

why.correct: The superior sagittal sinus runs along the top midline in the fold of dura between the two cerebral hemispheres. Cerebrospinal fluid drains into it through the arachnoid granulations.
options: Correct. It runs front to back along the top of the skull.
The transverse sinuses run sideways around the back of the skull, receiving blood from the superior sagittal sinus.
The sigmoid sinuses are the S-shaped channels at the base of the skull that become the internal jugular veins.
