The cavernous sinuses sit on each side of the sphenoid bone, deep in the skull base, not along the top.

why.correct: The hepatic portal vein forms behind the pancreas where the superior mesenteric and splenic veins join. It carries blood from the gut's capillaries to the liver's sinusoids.
options: The inferior vena cava receives blood from the liver through the hepatic veins, after the liver has processed it. No gut vein drains into it directly.
The superior mesenteric vein is a tributary of the pinned vein. It drains most of the intestines, while the pinned vessel collects from the stomach, spleen and pancreas as well.
Correct. The hepatic portal vein collects blood from all the gut organs and delivers it to the liver.
The splenic vein is the other main tributary. It drains the spleen and parts of the pancreas and stomach.

why.correct: Behind each sternoclavicular joint, the internal jugular and subclavian veins join to form a brachiocephalic vein. The right and left brachiocephalic veins then join to form the superior vena cava.
options: Correct. There are two brachiocephalic veins, unlike the single brachiocephalic trunk on the arterial side.
The superior vena cava is formed one step later, where the two brachiocephalic veins meet.
The azygos vein drains the chest wall and joins the back of the superior vena cava.
The external jugular vein is a superficial neck vein that drains into the subclavian vein.

why.correct: Blood in the superior sagittal sinus runs to the back of the skull, turns sideways into a transverse sinus, curves down as the sigmoid sinus and leaves the skull as the internal jugular vein. That joins the subclavian vein as the brachiocephalic vein, and the two brachiocephalic veins form the superior vena cava.

Intestinal capillaries drain into the superior mesenteric vein, which joins the splenic vein to form the hepatic portal vein. That vein branches to the liver's sinusoids, the second capillary bed. The sinusoids drain into the hepatic veins, which empty into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm.

Blood from the gut goes through the hepatic portal vein to the liver's sinusoids before it can reach the heart. The liver breaks down much of the drug on this first pass. IV drug in an arm vein goes to the heart and out to the body without passing through the liver first.
options: Correct. The hepatic portal system routes everything absorbed from the gut through the liver first.
Stomach acid does break down some drugs, but the question states that the liver removes most of this one. Acid alone does not explain a 90% loss.
Arm veins drain through the subclavian and brachiocephalic veins to the superior vena cava and the heart. They do not lead to the liver.
Gut veins do not drain into the inferior vena cava directly. Blood reaches it only after passing through the liver.

why.correct: The tibial and fibular veins of the calf join behind the knee as the popliteal vein, which continues up the thigh as the femoral vein.
options: The great saphenous vein is superficial. It joins the femoral vein near the groin but is not part of the deep chain from the calf.
Correct. The popliteal vein links the calf veins to the femoral vein.
The common iliac vein comes after the external iliac vein, higher up in the pelvis.
The deep femoral vein drains the thigh muscles into the femoral vein. It does not carry blood from the calf.

why.correct: The cephalic, basilic, great saphenous and external jugular veins run in the fat under the skin and have their own names. Deep veins such as the femoral and popliteal veins run beside arteries of the same name.
options: Correct. The cephalic vein runs up the thumb side of the arm under the skin.
The femoral vein is a deep vein beside the femoral artery.
Correct. The basilic vein runs up the inner forearm and arm under the skin before diving deep.
Correct. The great saphenous vein runs up the inner leg under the skin.
The popliteal vein is a deep vein behind the knee, beside the popliteal artery.
Correct. The external jugular vein runs across the side of the neck just under the skin.

why.correct: The superior vena cava sits on the right side, entering the right atrium. The left brachiocephalic vein has to cross in front of the arch's branches to reach it, so it is about two to three times as long as the right one.
options: The left arm's artery does arise differently, straight from the arch, but vein length is set by the route back to the heart, and the two arms drain the same way.
Correct. Crossing the midline makes the left vein longer.
The heart muscle drains mainly through the coronary sinus into the right atrium, not through the brachiocephalic veins.
The left brachiocephalic vein runs across the upper chest in front of the arch's branches. Its length comes from the distance to the right side, not from being pushed upward.

why.correct: Veins around the nose and upper lip connect with the cavernous sinus beside the sphenoid bone, and blood in them can flow toward the skull. Nerves to the eye muscles pass through or beside the cavernous sinus, so infection there causes eye swelling and double vision.
options: The superior sagittal sinus runs along the top of the skull. It is not directly connected to the face veins near the nose, and it is not beside the nerves to the eye muscles.
The external jugular vein drains the scalp and side of the face down into the neck, away from the skull.
Correct. Face veins near the nose link to the cavernous sinus.
The great saphenous vein is in the leg and has no connection to the face.

why.correct: The hepatic veins collect blood from the liver's sinusoids and drain into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm.
options: The hepatic portal vein carries blood into the liver, from the gut.
Correct. The hepatic veins are the liver's exits.
The superior mesenteric vein drains the intestines into the hepatic portal vein. It carries blood toward the liver.
The splenic vein drains the spleen into the hepatic portal vein. It also carries blood toward the liver.

why.correct: The subclavian vein first joins the internal jugular vein to form the right brachiocephalic vein. Only then do the right and left brachiocephalic veins form the superior vena cava.
options: This step is right. The cephalic vein starts from the network on the back of the hand, on the thumb side.
This step is right. The cephalic vein runs up the outer arm and drains into the axillary vein near the shoulder.
This step is right. The axillary vein is renamed subclavian at the outer edge of the first rib.
This is the error. A brachiocephalic vein sits between the subclavian vein and the superior vena cava.
This step is right. The superior vena cava enters the top of the right atrium.

why.correct: A scarred liver resists flow, so pressure rises in the hepatic portal vein and its tributaries. Blood takes detours through small connections to systemic veins, including those at the lower end of the esophagus. These veins swell and can rupture, causing heavy bleeding.
options: Correct. Backed-up portal blood reroutes through thin-walled veins that can bleed.
Veins do not drain into the aorta. Backed-up venous blood cannot reach an artery, and the liver scarring affects flow through the sinusoids, not the aorta.
Liver scarring affects the venous side, not the arteries to the stomach, and a dead stomach wall would not explain sudden heavy bleeding.
The portal vein forms behind the pancreas, outside the liver. Liver scarring does not stop it from forming; it raises the pressure inside it.

why.correct: A dural sinus is a channel between the two layers of the dura mater, lined by endothelium. Its wall has no smooth muscle and it has no valves; the stiff dura keeps it open.
options: Dural sinuses carry deoxygenated blood from the brain, like other systemic veins.
Correct. Its wall is dura, not a three-layered vessel wall.
A dural sinus has no tunica media at all. Its wall is made of dura.
Cerebrospinal fluid drains into the superior sagittal sinus and mixes with the blood there, but the sinuses carry venous blood.

why.correct: The external jugular vein runs just under the skin of the neck and drains through the subclavian and brachiocephalic veins to the superior vena cava. At 45 degrees it is normally flat. If it stays full, blood is backing up because pressure in the right atrium is high, as when blood around the heart squeezes it in cardiac tamponade.
options: Correct. A bulging external jugular vein reflects high pressure where the veins empty into the heart.
The internal jugular vein is deep, under a neck muscle, and it carries blood away from the brain, not to it.
The carotid artery is deep and pulses; it does not bulge as a full, soft vein.
The vertebral veins run inside the holes of the neck vertebrae and cannot be seen.

why.correct: The second number is diastolic pressure: the lowest pressure in the large arteries, reached at the end of diastole just before the ventricle ejects again.
options: Correct. Diastolic pressure is the trough of the arterial pressure wave.
Venous pressure is much lower, near 0 to 15 mm Hg. Both numbers in a reading are arterial pressures.
The average over the cycle is the mean arterial pressure, which for 118/76 is about 90 mm Hg, not 76.
Pressure inside the relaxed left ventricle during diastole is only a few mm Hg. The aortic valve is shut, so the artery keeps its own, much higher pressure.

why.correct: Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic = 150 − 70 = 80 mm Hg.
options: 70 mm Hg is his diastolic pressure, not the difference between the two numbers.
Correct. 150 − 70 = 80 mm Hg.
97 mm Hg is roughly his mean arterial pressure: 70 + 80 ÷ 3 ≈ 97.
110 mm Hg is halfway between the two numbers, the simple average. It is not the difference.

why.correct: Pulse pressure = 110 − 68 = 42 mm Hg. One-third of it is 14 mm Hg. MAP ≈ 68 + 14 = 82 mm Hg.
options: 89 mm Hg is halfway between the two numbers. At rest, the arteries spend more time near diastolic pressure, so the mean is lower than halfway.
96 mm Hg adds two-thirds of the pulse pressure to the diastolic value, weighting the peak too heavily.
Correct. 68 + 42 ÷ 3 = 82 mm Hg.
42 mm Hg is the pulse pressure, not the mean pressure.

why.correct: The one-third weighting assumes the arteries spend about two-thirds of each cycle near diastolic pressure, which fits resting heart rates. At fast rates diastole shortens far more than systole, so a larger share of each cycle is spent near the peak. The true mean is higher than the estimate of 80 + 80 ÷ 3 ≈ 107 mm Hg.
options: The one-third rule is fitted to resting heart rates. How well it matches depends on how each cycle is split between systole and diastole, and a sprint changes that split.
An overestimate would need more time spent near diastolic pressure. A fast heart rate does the opposite: diastole shrinks.
The formula can be applied at any rate: her pulse pressure is 160 − 80 = 80 mm Hg. The problem is that its one-third weighting no longer fits.
Correct. With diastole shortened, the true mean is higher than the resting formula predicts.

why.correct: A stiff aorta cannot stretch to absorb each ejection, so systolic pressure climbs higher. It also stores less stretch, so it recoils less during diastole, and diastolic pressure falls lower. Pulse pressure widens from 40 to 90 mm Hg.
options: A much larger stroke volume would raise systolic pressure, but it would not by itself lower the diastolic pressure. Stroke volume usually does not rise with age.
Correct. Loss of elastic stretch and recoil raises the peak and lowers the trough.
Wider arterioles would lower resistance and tend to lower both numbers, not raise systolic pressure by 40 mm Hg.
Veins carry blood toward the heart, and valves in the heart and veins prevent it being pushed back into arteries.
633 mL/min comes from 95 ÷ 0.15, using the arterial pressure alone instead of the pressure difference.
13.5 mL/min comes from multiplying 90 by 0.15. Flow is the pressure difference divided by resistance.
Correct. 90 ÷ 0.15 = 600 mL/min.
667 mL/min comes from adding the two pressures (100 ÷ 0.15). Flow depends on their difference.

why.correct: Resistance depends on 1 ÷ radius⁴. Halving the radius makes radius⁴ one-sixteenth as large, so resistance becomes 16 times larger. With the same pressure difference, flow becomes one-sixteenth: 200 ÷ 16 = 12.5 mL/min.
options: Halving flow would treat resistance as depending on the radius alone, not its fourth power.
One-quarter of the flow would treat resistance as depending on radius squared.
One-eighth of the flow would treat resistance as depending on radius cubed.
Correct. (½)⁴ = 1/16, so flow falls to 200 ÷ 16 = 12.5 mL/min.

why.correct: Vasodilation widens the arterioles, and through the fourth-power rule resistance falls sharply. With the same driving pressure, flow to the muscle rises. Less pressure is lost across the arterioles, so capillary pressure in that bed rises, and total peripheral resistance falls slightly because the bed is in parallel with all the others.

variables.name: Radius of the calf muscle's arterioles
variables.why: Relaxed smooth muscle in the arteriole wall lets the vessel widen: vasodilation.

variables.name: Resistance of the calf muscle's vascular bed
variables.why: Resistance depends on 1 ÷ radius⁴, so a wider radius lowers resistance steeply.

variables.name: Blood flow through the calf muscle
variables.why: By F = ΔP / R, with the pressure difference unchanged and resistance lower, flow rises.

variables.name: Pressure in the calf muscle's capillaries
variables.why: Less pressure is used up across the wider arterioles, so more of the arterial pressure reaches the capillaries downstream.

variables.name: Total peripheral resistance
variables.why: The calf bed is one of many beds in parallel. Lowering the resistance of one lowers the total a little.

why.correct: Elastic stretch and recoil damp the pressure swing. Without them, the peak rises and the trough falls, so pulse pressure widens.

variables.name: Systolic pressure
variables.why: A stiff aorta stretches less to take in each ejection, so the same volume raises the pressure more.

variables.name: Diastolic pressure
variables.why: Less stretch is stored during ejection, so there is less recoil to hold pressure up during diastole.

variables.name: Pulse pressure
variables.why: Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic. A higher peak and a lower trough widen the gap.

why.correct: The steepest drop, from about 85 to about 35 mm Hg, is across the arterioles. The same flow passes every level, and by F = ΔP / R the level with the largest resistance uses up the largest pressure difference. Arterioles hold the largest share of the resistance.
options: Single capillaries are narrow, but billions of them lie in parallel, so their combined resistance is smaller than that of the arterioles. The graph shows a smaller drop across them.
Correct. Arterioles are the resistance vessels, so the pressure falls most across them.
The graph shows a slow, gentle fall through the veins. Valves stop backflow; they do not create a large resistance to forward flow.
The mean pressure in the aorta is almost flat on the graph. Stretching stores energy that is returned during diastole.

why.correct: Velocity = flow ÷ total cross-sectional area. The same total flow passes through every level each minute, and the capillaries together have the greatest total area, so blood moves slowest there. The velocity curve is the mirror image of the area curve.
options: Correct. Largest total area means lowest velocity for the same flow.
A narrow single tube would speed blood up, not slow it, if it were the only path. What matters is the total area of all the capillaries side by side.
Pressure is still about 35 mm Hg entering the capillaries, and velocity rises again in the veins where pressure is even lower. Low velocity is not caused by the push running out.
In a closed circuit, the same total volume per minute flows through all the capillaries together as through the aorta.

why.correct: The first Korotkoff sound appears when cuff pressure just falls below the peak of the arterial wave, at about 120 mm Hg, so that is systolic pressure. The sounds stop when cuff pressure falls below the trough, at about 80 mm Hg: the artery then stays open and flow is smooth, so that is diastolic pressure.
options: 130 is where the cuff pressure starts, above the peaks of the wave, when no sound is heard yet. The first sound comes at about 120.
The sounds stop when cuff pressure reaches about 80. Cuff pressures near 70 come after the last sound, when the artery is already open all the time.
Correct. First sound = systolic, about 120; last sound = diastolic, about 80.
This reverses the two. Cuff pressure falls during the reading, so the first sound is at the higher, systolic pressure.

why.correct: A cuff that is too small cannot spread its pressure over the whole artery, so it needs extra pressure to squeeze the artery shut. Both the first and last sounds occur at a higher cuff pressure than the true arterial pressure, so the reading is too high.
options: A cuff that is too large tends to read low. A too-small cuff has the opposite effect.
The gauge measures the cuff's pressure, not the artery's. The two match only when the cuff transmits its pressure fully to the artery, which a small cuff does not.
Correct. An undersized cuff overestimates blood pressure.
The same error affects both sounds, because both depend on the cuff squeezing the artery closed.

why.correct: Convert flow: 6 L/min = 6,000 cm³/min = 100 cm³/s. Velocity = flow ÷ area = 100 ÷ 4,000 = 0.025 cm/s, a quarter of a millimeter per second.
options: Correct. 100 cm³/s ÷ 4,000 cm² = 0.025 cm/s.
1.5 cm/s comes from 6,000 ÷ 4,000, using flow per minute while calling the answer per second.
0.67 cm/s comes from dividing area by flow (4,000 ÷ 6,000). Velocity is flow divided by area.
25 cm/s is a typical speed in the aorta, where the cross-sectional area is about a thousand times smaller.

why.correct: Resistance depends on the vessel's radius (to the fourth power), its length and the viscosity of the blood. The pressure difference and the speed of blood are results of flow, not properties of the vessel that set resistance.
options: Correct. Radius has the largest effect, through the fourth-power rule.
The pressure difference drives flow through the resistance; it does not set the resistance itself.
Correct. A longer vessel has proportionally more resistance.
Correct. Thicker blood, with a higher hematocrit, has more resistance.
Velocity depends on flow and cross-sectional area. It is an outcome, not one of the factors in Poiseuille's law.

why.correct: The cuff first closes the artery completely. As cuff pressure falls below the peak of each wave, spurts of turbulent flow make the Korotkoff sounds, marking systolic pressure. They continue while the artery opens and closes with each beat, and stop when cuff pressure falls below the trough, marking diastolic pressure.
Viscosity depends mostly on the hematocrit. With fewer red cells, blood is less viscous, resistance falls, and by F = ΔP / R the same pressure difference drives more flow.
options: Her blood carries less oxygen, but oxygen content is not part of the flow equation. Flow falls only if resistance rises or the pressure difference falls, and neither has happened.
Flow depends on the pressure difference and the resistance. Viscosity is part of resistance, so a change in viscosity changes flow even with the same pressure difference.
Correct. Fewer red cells make the blood less viscous, resistance falls, and F = ΔP / R rises.

why.correct: R = ΔP / F. ΔP = 90 − 0 = 90 mm Hg. R = 90 ÷ 4.5 = 20 mm Hg·min/L.
options: 405 comes from multiplying 90 by 4.5. Resistance is the pressure difference divided by the flow.
0.05 comes from dividing flow by pressure (4.5 ÷ 90), which is the inverse of resistance.
94.5 comes from adding the pressure and the flow, which have different units and cannot be added.

why.correct: Pressure falls steadily all the way around the circuit, because blood always flows from higher to lower pressure. In the capillaries it continues to fall, from about 35 to about 15 mm Hg. Slower velocity does not raise the pressure.
options: This step is right. The aorta carries the full pulsing pressure from the left ventricle.
This step is right. Large arteries are wide and have little resistance, so little pressure is used up across them.
This step is right. The arterioles hold the largest share of the resistance, and they damp out the pulse.
This is the error. Pressure keeps falling through the capillaries; blood could not flow on into the venules if it rose.
This step is right. The wide veins need only a small pressure difference to carry the full flow.

why.correct: 26 cm × 0.77 mm Hg per cm ≈ 20 mm Hg. The weight of the column of blood above the cuff adds to the pressure through the whole cycle, so both numbers rise: 124 + 20 = 144 and 78 + 20 = 98.
options: This would be right only with the arm supported at heart level.
Correct. Both numbers are about 20 mm Hg too high.
Pressure would read low only if the arm were raised above the heart.
The column of blood adds pressure at every point in the cycle, so diastolic pressure rises too.

why.correct: CO = HR × SV = 80 beats/min × 65 mL/beat = 5,200 mL/min = 5.2 L/min.
options: 145 comes from adding heart rate and stroke volume. Cardiac output is their product.
Correct. 80 × 65 = 5,200 mL/min, which is 5.2 L/min.
1.2 L/min comes from dividing heart rate by stroke volume (80 ÷ 65). Multiply them instead.
52 L/min is ten times too large: 5,200 mL is 5.2 L, not 52 L.

why.correct: Rearrange CO = HR × SV to SV = CO ÷ HR. Convert 6.0 L/min to 6,000 mL/min. SV = 6,000 ÷ 75 = 80 mL per beat.
options: 450 comes from multiplying 6.0 by 75. Stroke volume is cardiac output divided by heart rate.
12.5 comes from 75 ÷ 6, dividing the wrong way round.
0.8 comes from 6.0 ÷ 75 without converting liters to milliliters. The answer is in liters: 0.08 L, which is 80 mL.
Correct. 6,000 mL/min ÷ 75 beats/min = 80 mL per beat.

why.correct: A beta blocker removes the sympathetic push on both the SA node and the ventricular muscle. Heart rate and contractility fall. Longer diastoles improve filling a little, which partly offsets the fall in stroke volume, but cardiac output ends up lower.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: With beta-1 receptor proteins blocked, norepinephrine cannot steepen the pacemaker potential, so the SA node reaches threshold more slowly.

variables.name: Contractility
variables.why: Blocking beta-1 receptor proteins on ventricular cells lowers cyclic AMP, so less calcium enters through L-type channels and less is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

variables.name: Filling time
variables.why: A slower heart rate lengthens each diastole, so the ventricles have longer to fill.

variables.name: Cardiac output
variables.why: Heart rate falls, and the slightly better filling does not fully make up for it and for the weaker contraction, so the product HR × SV falls.

why.correct: More venous return raises preload. Through the Frank–Starling mechanism, the stretched ventricle ejects more, so stroke volume and cardiac output rise without any change in heart rate.

variables.name: End-diastolic volume
variables.why: More venous return fills the ventricles more during diastole.

variables.name: Stretch of ventricular muscle (preload)
variables.why: A larger end-diastolic volume stretches the ventricular wall further.

variables.name: Stroke volume
variables.why: By the Frank–Starling mechanism, the more-stretched ventricle contracts more forcefully and ejects more.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Venous return acts on filling and stretch, not directly on the SA node, so heart rate does not change before a reflex acts.

variables.name: Cardiac output
variables.why: Stroke volume has risen at the same heart rate, so HR × SV is larger.

why.correct: The nervous system raises sympathetic and lowers parasympathetic drive to the heart, and working skeletal muscles push more blood back through the veins. Heart rate rises, contractility rises and filling improves, so stroke volume and cardiac output both rise.

variables.name: Sympathetic activity to the heart
variables.why: Signals from the motor cortex and from sensory receptors in moving muscles and joints reach the cardiovascular center, which increases cardioaccelerator output and reduces vagal output.

variables.name: Venous return
variables.why: Rhythmic contraction of the leg muscles squeezes the deep veins (the skeletal muscle pump), and deeper breathing strengthens the respiratory pump.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Less vagal tone and more norepinephrine on the SA node steepen the pacemaker potential.

variables.name: End-systolic volume
variables.why: Sympathetic stimulation raises contractility, so the ventricle squeezes out more of its blood.

variables.name: Stroke volume
variables.why: Greater venous return raises EDV and greater contractility lowers ESV, so EDV − ESV rises.

variables.name: Cardiac output
variables.why: Both heart rate and stroke volume rise, so their product rises several-fold.

why.correct: Norepinephrine on beta-1 receptor proteins increases the funny current and calcium entry, so the pacemaker potential is steeper and reaches threshold sooner. More action potentials fit into each second, so heart rate rises.
options: The dashed threshold line sits at the same level, about minus 40 mV, in all three traces.
The action potentials are not longer in the sympathetic trace; there are simply more of them in the same time.
Correct. A faster climb to threshold means more frequent firing.
The peaks reach about the same height in all three traces. Peak height does not set the rate.

why.correct: Acetylcholine on muscarinic receptor proteins opens extra potassium channels, so each cycle starts from about minus 70 instead of minus 60 mV. It also reduces the funny current, so the climb is shallower. Starting lower and climbing slower both delay reaching threshold.
options: Correct. A lower start and a gentler slope together lengthen the time to threshold.
The threshold line is unchanged, and the action potentials reach about the same peak.
The trace spends longer below threshold, not longer depolarized, and the threshold does not move.
The trace shows a slow climb, not a pause at threshold. Once threshold is reached, the cell fires at once.

why.correct: Resting cardiac sarcomeres are shorter than optimal. Stretch brings them closer to optimal overlap, and it makes troponin bind calcium more readily, so the same calcium release switches on more cross-bridges. This is the Frank–Starling mechanism, and it works even in a heart with no nerve supply.
options: The Frank–Starling mechanism needs no nerves or hormones; it works in an isolated heart. A sympathetic effect would be a change in contractility, a different curve.
Correct. Better overlap and greater calcium sensitivity explain the stronger contraction.
The main effect of stretch is on how the contractile proteins respond to calcium, not on how much calcium enters through L-type channels.
The strength of contraction depends on how many cross-bridges are active, not mainly on how long the plateau lasts.

why.correct: The extra blood from the right ventricle crosses the lungs and returns to the left atrium. The left ventricle fills more, its EDV and stretch rise, and by the Frank–Starling mechanism it ejects more until its output equals the right's.
options: Heart rate is shared by both ventricles, because one SA node drives them. The vagus cannot slow one ventricle alone, and the question says nerve signals did not change.
Semilunar valves open and close passively with pressure differences. They do not partly close to regulate flow.
Correct. The extra blood stretches the left ventricle, which then ejects more, matching the right ventricle's output beat by beat.
A hormone would change contractility, and the question describes a match restored within a few beats without any change in signals. Stretch alone does it.

why.correct: A narrowed aortic valve raises afterload. The ventricle spends longer building pressure before ejection, less contraction is left for ejecting, and more blood remains at the end of systole: ESV rises and stroke volume falls.
options: Filling happens through the mitral valve during diastole. Afterload acts during ejection, so its first effect is on how much is left, not how much comes in.
The ventricle does work harder, but against a higher pressure it ejects less, not more. ESV falls only if contractility rises enough to overcome the load.
Correct. Higher afterload leaves more blood in the ventricle after ejection.
The question describes a narrowed valve, not a leaking one. Backflow would be a different problem.

why.correct: Afterload is the pressure the ventricle must exceed to open its semilunar valve and eject blood. For the left ventricle it is set mainly by aortic pressure.
options: That is preload, the stretch before contraction.
Correct. Afterload is the load faced during ejection.
That is end-systolic volume, which afterload affects but which is not the same thing.
That is contractility, the strength of contraction independent of stretch.

why.correct: Norepinephrine and epinephrine act through beta-1 receptor proteins to raise the calcium available to the cross-bridges, and thyroid hormones also raise contractility. Hyperkalemia, calcium channel blockers and acidosis all weaken contraction.
options: Correct. This is the main positive inotropic signal.
Hyperkalemia depolarizes cardiac cells and weakens their action potentials, lowering contractility.
Correct. Epinephrine acts on the same beta-1 receptor proteins as norepinephrine.
A calcium channel blocker reduces calcium entry through L-type channels, lowering contractility.
Correct. Thyroid hormones raise contractility and heart rate.
Acidosis weakens the contractile proteins' response to calcium, lowering contractility.

why.correct: The vagus nerve releases acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptor proteins on SA node cells, which slows the pacemaker potential. Blocking those receptor proteins removes vagal tone, so the pacemaker potential climbs faster and heart rate rises toward the SA node's own rate.
options: A fall would need more vagal effect or less sympathetic effect. Atropine removes vagal effect, and it does not block the beta-1 receptor proteins that carry sympathetic signals.
Correct. Atropine blocks the muscarinic receptor proteins through which the vagus slows the SA node, so the pacemaker potential climbs faster.
The SA node does carry muscarinic receptor proteins; that is how the vagus nerve slows it. Blocking them removes vagal tone and changes the rate.

why.correct: Norepinephrine binds beta-1 receptor proteins, raising cyclic AMP. That lets more calcium in through L-type channels and triggers more calcium-induced calcium release. More calcium on troponin allows more cross-bridges, a stronger contraction, a smaller end-systolic volume and a larger stroke volume.

Most of the shortening at fast rates comes out of diastole. At 220 beats/min, filling time is so short that EDV and stroke volume collapse. Stroke volume fell by a third while heart rate rose by only a fifth, so HR × SV fell.
options: SA node action potentials are all-or-none and do not weaken. Here the rhythm is fast because impulses are frequent, not weak.
Correct. Filling time limits stroke volume at very high heart rates.
Afterload depends on arterial pressure, which does not rise because of the rate itself. The problem is filling, not ejection.
Nothing in the scenario suggests forceful contraction; a smaller stroke volume shows the opposite.

why.correct: Cardiac reserve = highest cardiac output − resting cardiac output = 13.5 − 4.5 = 9.0 L/min.
options: Correct. 13.5 − 4.5 = 9.0 L/min.
18.0 comes from adding the two values. Reserve is the difference.
3.0 is the ratio of highest to resting output (13.5 ÷ 4.5), not the difference.
13.5 is his highest output, not the extra above rest.

why.correct: Parasympathetic fibers are cholinergic. The vagus nerves release acetylcholine, which binds muscarinic receptor proteins on SA node cells. Norepinephrine is the sympathetic transmitter and speeds the heart.
options: This step is right. The cardioinhibitory center drives the parasympathetic supply to the heart.
This step is right. The vagus nerves carry the parasympathetic fibers to the heart.
This is the error. The vagus releases acetylcholine, not norepinephrine.
This step is right. Acetylcholine opens potassium channels and reduces the funny current.
This step is right. Starting lower and climbing slower delays threshold, so heart rate falls.

why.correct: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume: beats per minute times milliliters per beat gives milliliters per minute.
options: Correct. HR × SV.
End-diastolic volume is how much the ventricle holds, not how much it ejects. Not all of it leaves each beat.
Ejection fraction is a proportion with no volume unit, so heart rate times ejection fraction cannot give a volume per minute.
Mean arterial pressure is a pressure, not a volume per beat.

why.correct: Before: SV = 130 − 60 = 70 mL. After: SV = 130 − 40 = 90 mL. Stroke volume rose by 20 mL, all from a smaller end-systolic volume.
options: 10 mL would be half the fall in ESV. The whole 20 mL fall in ESV adds to stroke volume, because EDV did not change.
Correct. 90 − 70 = 20 mL.
A fall in ESV means more blood was ejected, so stroke volume rises.
40 mL is the new ESV, not the change in stroke volume.

why.correct: The cardiovascular center is a network of neurons in the medulla oblongata of the brainstem. It sends sympathetic output through the cardiac accelerator nerves and parasympathetic output through the vagus nerves.
options: The hypothalamus influences the cardiovascular center, for example during fear, but the center itself is in the medulla oblongata.
The cerebral cortex can influence heart rate through higher centers, but it does not contain the cardiovascular center.
Correct. The medulla oblongata houses the cardiovascular center.
The SA node is the heart's own pacemaker, which the cardiovascular center adjusts. It is not part of the brain.

why.correct: Walking increases venous return through the muscle pump, so the transplanted heart fills more and ejects more by the Frank–Starling mechanism, which needs no nerves. Epinephrine released into the blood by the adrenal medulla reaches the heart's beta-1 receptor proteins and raises heart rate and contractility. The hormone takes time to build up, which is why the rise is slower.
options: Correct. Stretch and a blood-borne hormone both work without nerves.
The vagus nerve and the cardioaccelerator center both act through nerves, which the transplanted heart lacks.
The cardiac plexus nerves were cut during the transplant, and acetylcholine from the vagus would slow the heart rather than raise output.
The cardioinhibitory center acts through the vagus nerve, which is cut. A longer filling time would come from a slower rate, which is not what happens.

why.correct: Blood colloid osmotic pressure is the osmotic pull of plasma proteins, mainly albumin, that cannot cross the capillary wall easily. It draws water toward the plasma, into the capillary.
options: Capillary hydrostatic pressure is the push of blood against the capillary wall. It drives fluid out of the capillary, not in.
Correct. Plasma proteins stay in the capillary and pull water toward themselves, into the blood.
Interstitial fluid colloid osmotic pressure comes from the small amount of protein between the cells. It pulls fluid toward the interstitial fluid, out of the capillary.
Systolic pressure is the peak pressure in the large arteries. By the time blood reaches a capillary, much of it has been lost across the arterioles, and it is not one of the four Starling forces.

why.correct: Outward forces: CHP + IFCOP = 30 + 4 = 34 mm Hg. Inward forces: BCOP + IFHP = 26 + 2 = 28 mm Hg. NFP = 34 − 28 = +6 mm Hg. A positive value means filtration.
options: This has the right size but the wrong sign. The outward forces (34 mm Hg) are larger than the inward forces (28 mm Hg), so the result is positive, which means filtration.
This comes from adding the interstitial hydrostatic pressure to the outward side instead of the inward side. IFHP pushes fluid into the capillary, so it belongs with BCOP.
Correct. (30 + 4) − (26 + 2) = +6 mm Hg, so fluid filters out.
This comes from subtracting IFHP from CHP but leaving out IFCOP: (30 − 2) − 26. IFCOP pulls fluid out of the capillary, so it must be added to the outward side.

why.correct: Outward: CHP + IFCOP = 18 + 3 = 21 mm Hg. Inward: BCOP + IFHP = 25 + 1 = 26 mm Hg. NFP = 21 − 26 = −5 mm Hg. The negative sign means the forces favor reabsorption at this point; in the revised Starling principle, that inward flow does not last at steady state.
options: This is BCOP − CHP (25 − 18): it subtracts in the wrong direction and leaves out both interstitial forces. Subtract the inward total from the outward total.
This treats IFCOP as an inward force: (18 − 3) − (25 − 1) = −9. IFCOP pulls fluid toward the interstitial fluid, so it adds to the outward side.
This has the right size but the wrong sign. The inward forces (26 mm Hg) exceed the outward forces (21 mm Hg), so the result is negative.

why.correct: The liver makes albumin, the protein that supplies most of blood colloid osmotic pressure. With less albumin, less pull holds fluid in the capillaries, net filtration pressure rises, and fluid collects in the interstitial spaces. Her ankles swell first because they sit lowest when she is upright.
options: A rise in capillary pressure causes edema, but nothing in this case raises it. The finding that points to the cause is her low albumin.
Leaky capillaries cause the swelling of inflammation. Her problem is too little protein in the blood, not protein escaping through the wall.
Correct. Low albumin lowers the inward pull, so more fluid filters out and stays in the tissue.
Interstitial hydrostatic pressure rises, not falls, as fluid collects in the tissue. That rise is a result of the edema, and it pushes back against more filtration.

why.correct: Injury triggers inflammation. Histamine and related chemicals widen the clefts between endothelial cells, so plasma proteins escape into the interstitial fluid. Interstitial oncotic pressure rises, the inward oncotic pull across the wall shrinks, and fluid filters out faster. The same chemicals dilate the ankle's arterioles, which raises capillary pressure there and adds to it.
options: Correct. Increased permeability lets protein leak out, and the loss of the oncotic difference drives the swelling.
His blood pressure is normal, and a change in arterial pressure would not cause swelling in one ankle only. The cause is local.
Albumin is made by the liver and carried in plasma, not released by injured cells. A rise in blood colloid osmotic pressure would pull fluid into the capillaries and reduce swelling.
Closing capillaries would lower flow and filtration in the ankle. The swelling is interstitial fluid that filtered out, not blood trapped in the tissue.

why.correct: An osmotic pull across a barrier needs a solute that stays on one side. Sodium passes through the clefts between endothelial cells, so plasma and interstitial fluid end up with nearly the same sodium concentration and no lasting difference. Proteins are held back, so they make a concentration difference, and that difference pulls water into the capillary.
options: Endothelial cells do not pump sodium out of capillaries to set up a gradient. Sodium moves freely through the clefts.
Charged particles such as sodium do cause osmosis across membranes that block them, for example the plasma membrane of a cell. The point is whether the solute crosses this particular barrier.
Osmotic pressure depends on the number of dissolved particles, not their mass. By number, sodium ions far outnumber proteins.
Correct. Only solutes that cannot cross the capillary wall create a lasting osmotic difference across it.

why.correct: Filtration rises when capillary hydrostatic pressure rises (dilated arterioles, higher venous pressure), when blood colloid osmotic pressure falls (less albumin), or when protein leaks out and shrinks the oncotic difference (leaky walls).
options: Increases filtration. Dilated arterioles lose less pressure, so more pressure reaches the capillaries and CHP rises.
Increases filtration. With no large resistance between capillaries and veins, a rise in venous pressure passes back into the capillaries and raises CHP.
Increases filtration. Less albumin means a lower blood colloid osmotic pressure, so less inward pull opposes filtration.
Decreases filtration. Constricted arterioles lose more pressure, so CHP downstream falls.
Decreases filtration. More albumin raises the inward oncotic pull.
Increases filtration. Protein leaking into the interstitial fluid raises IFCOP and shrinks the oncotic difference that holds fluid in the blood.

why.correct: Less plasma protein lowers blood colloid osmotic pressure. Filtration then exceeds drainage, interstitial fluid collects, and its pressure rises until a new balance is reached with visible edema.

variables.name: Blood colloid osmotic pressure
variables.why: Plasma proteins, mainly albumin, create blood colloid osmotic pressure. Fewer proteins means less osmotic pull.

variables.name: Capillary hydrostatic pressure
variables.why: Capillary hydrostatic pressure depends on arterial pressure, arteriole resistance and venous pressure. None of these is changed directly by the protein level.

variables.name: Net filtration pressure
variables.why: With less inward oncotic pull and unchanged outward push, the balance of the four forces shifts toward filtration.

variables.name: Interstitial fluid volume
variables.why: More fluid filters out than drains away, so fluid collects between the cells: edema.

variables.name: Interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure
variables.why: As fluid collects in the tissue spaces, the pressure of that fluid rises. This rise partly opposes further filtration.

why.correct: Gravity raises venous pressure in the feet, which raises capillary hydrostatic pressure. With the oncotic pull unchanged, net filtration rises and fluid collects in the feet.

variables.name: Venous pressure at the ankle
variables.why: Standing adds the weight of the column of blood above the ankle, and without walking the skeletal muscle pump does not empty the leg veins.

variables.name: Capillary hydrostatic pressure in the feet
variables.why: No large resistance separates the capillaries from the veins, so the rise in venous pressure passes back into the capillaries.

variables.name: Blood colloid osmotic pressure
variables.why: Standing does not change the amount of protein in her plasma, so the inward oncotic pull is about the same.

variables.name: Fluid in the tissues of her feet
variables.why: Higher capillary pressure raises net filtration, so fluid collects in the tissues and her shoes feel tight.

why.correct: Right after the bleed, whole blood is gone but its composition is unchanged. Lower capillary pressure then lets protein-poor interstitial fluid move into the plasma for a few minutes. After that, the capillaries keep filtering less than before while the separate drainage route keeps returning fluid, so the plasma keeps gaining fluid for hours. That restores some plasma volume and dilutes the red cells and proteins, so hematocrit and protein concentration fall hours later.

variables.name: Capillary hydrostatic pressure, right after the bleed
variables.why: Losing blood lowers arterial pressure, and the reflexes that follow constrict the arterioles, so less pressure reaches the capillaries.

variables.name: Hematocrit, right after the bleed
variables.why: The wound lost whole blood, cells and plasma in the same proportion, so the fraction of blood made of red cells has not changed yet.

variables.name: Net movement of interstitial fluid into the plasma, in the first hour
variables.why: With capillary pressure below the effective oncotic pull, fluid is reabsorbed into the blood for a limited time until proteins build up beneath the glycocalyx and stop it.

variables.name: Hematocrit, several hours later
variables.why: Interstitial fluid, which contains no red cells, has been added to the plasma. After the brief inward flow stops, filtration stays lower than before while drainage continues, so the plasma keeps gaining cell-free fluid. The remaining red cells are now spread through more fluid.

variables.name: Plasma protein concentration, several hours later
variables.why: The fluid drawn in from the interstitial spaces is low in protein, so it dilutes the plasma proteins until the liver makes more over the following days.

why.correct: Protein lost in the urine lowers plasma albumin, which lowers blood colloid osmotic pressure. With less inward pull, net filtration rises. Once filtration outpaces drainage, fluid collects, and gravity makes it show first in the feet and ankles.
options: The starting event: damaged kidneys let albumin pass into the urine.
Losing albumin faster than the liver replaces it lowers its concentration in plasma.
Albumin supplies most of blood colloid osmotic pressure, so less albumin means less inward pull.
With a smaller inward force and an unchanged outward push, the net filtration pressure becomes larger.
Faster filtration eventually exceeds the rate at which the tissue can drain.
The excess fluid is edema. Gravity pulls it toward the feet and ankles when the person is upright.

why.correct: When plasma proteins leak into the interstitial fluid, the protein concentration there goes up, so interstitial fluid colloid osmotic pressure rises. That rise pulls fluid out of the capillaries and shrinks the oncotic difference holding fluid in the blood.
options: Correct as written. Histamine is released from mast cells in injured or stung tissue.
Correct as written. Histamine makes endothelial cells pull apart, widening the clefts between them.
Correct as written. Wider gaps let large plasma proteins escape.
This is the wrong step. More protein in the interstitial fluid raises its colloid osmotic pressure; it does not lower it.
Correct as written. A higher IFCOP favors filtration, so fluid collects faster than it drains away.

why.correct: Outward filtration normally washes the thin space beneath the glycocalyx, keeping its protein level near zero. Once flow reverses, the washing stops, interstitial proteins diffuse into that space, and its oncotic pressure rises. The effective oncotic pull into the blood shrinks, and the inward flow dies away.
options: Correct. Protein accumulation beneath the glycocalyx cancels the inward oncotic pull.
The glycocalyx holds plasma proteins back whichever way fluid flows. Loss of plasma protein is not what stops reabsorption.
Arteriole diameter is set by local and nervous signals, not by the direction of flow across the capillary wall. Reabsorption fades even when capillary pressure stays low.
The glycocalyx stays in place. It is damaged in some diseases, but that is not part of the normal shutoff.

why.correct: At steady state, most capillaries filter along their whole length and do not keep reabsorbing at their venule ends. The filtered fluid is carried away by a separate set of thin-walled drainage vessels that empty into large veins near the heart. You will meet them in the lymphatic system.
options: This is the classic textbook picture, and exams often expect it. Direct measurements show that sustained venule-end reabsorption does not occur in most tissues.
Cells do not store filtered fluid and release it on dying. Interstitial fluid is drained continuously.
Correct. A separate drainage route returns the filtered fluid to the veins.
Water lost through the skin comes from the body's water as a whole. It is not the route that returns capillary filtrate to the blood.

why.correct: In the classic picture, capillary hydrostatic pressure falls along the capillary while blood colloid osmotic pressure stays about 25 mm Hg. At the venule end, the oncotic pull is larger, so the model predicts net reabsorption of most of the fluid filtered upstream.
options: That describes the arteriole end, where hydrostatic pressure is highest.
Correct for the classic model. The revised Starling principle shows this reabsorption is not sustained in most tissues, but this is the answer exams expect.
The classic model places the point of no net movement near the middle of the capillary, where CHP equals BCOP, not at the venule end.
Capillary hydrostatic pressure is lowest at the venule end, and a larger CHP would favor filtration, not reabsorption.

why.correct: Capillary pressure sits between arterial and venous pressure, closer to venous, because most of the pressure drop happens in the arterioles upstream. An arterial rise is mostly used up crossing that resistance. There is little resistance between capillaries and veins, so a venous rise passes back into the capillaries almost fully.
options: Veins have thinner walls than arteries, and wall thickness is not what decides how a pressure change reaches the capillaries.
Blood colloid osmotic pressure depends on plasma protein concentration. Arterial pressure does not change it.
Arterial and venous blood carry nearly the same protein concentration, because proteins are held back at the capillary wall.
Correct. The position of the main resistance, upstream of the capillaries, decides which pressure change reaches them.

why.correct: Small water-soluble solutes cross continuous capillaries through the water-filled clefts between endothelial cells. In the brain those clefts are sealed, so a water-soluble drug cannot take that route and stays mostly in the blood. Lipid-soluble substances such as oxygen can still cross by passing through the cells.
options: Sinusoids are the leakiest capillaries, found in places such as the liver and bone marrow. If brain capillaries were sinusoids, the drug would enter easily.
Correct. Sealed clefts block the main route for water-soluble solutes.
Hydrostatic pressure drives bulk flow of fluid, and the brain's capillary pressure is not unusually high. The drug's problem is the route through the wall.
Every capillary wall is made of endothelium. The difference is how tightly the endothelial cells are joined.

why.correct: Diffusion rate rises with surface area and falls with distance. When more capillaries in a working muscle carry blood, the total exchange surface grows and each cell is closer to an open capillary, so oxygen diffuses to the cells faster.
options: Oxygen leaves capillaries by diffusion down its concentration gradient. Bulk flow carries only a tiny fraction of the oxygen that diffusion moves.
Correct. More open capillaries means more area and a shorter path.
A thicker wall would lengthen the diffusion distance and slow oxygen delivery, and capillary walls do not thicken during a sprint.
Plasma proteins mostly stay in the blood, and oxygen does not need a carrier to cross the wall. It dissolves through the endothelial cells.

why.correct: Lipid-soluble substances such as oxygen and carbon dioxide dissolve in the phospholipid bilayer and cross straight through the endothelial cells. Water-soluble solutes such as glucose and sodium use the water-filled clefts. Albumin is mostly held back.
options: Crosses through the cells. Oxygen is small and lipid-soluble, so it dissolves in the bilayer.
Uses the clefts. Glucose is water-soluble and does not cross the bilayer easily.
Crosses through the cells. Carbon dioxide is lipid-soluble, like oxygen.
Uses the clefts. Charged ions cannot dissolve in the lipid bilayer.
Mostly held back. Albumin is too large for the clefts of a continuous capillary; a small amount crosses by transcytosis.

why.correct: Constricted arterioles lose more pressure, so less pressure reaches the capillaries and CHP falls. Filtration slows, and if CHP drops below the effective oncotic pull, interstitial fluid moves into the blood until protein builds up beneath the glycocalyx and stops it.
options: Correct. Lower capillary pressure slows filtration and can cause temporary reabsorption.
Constriction upstream lowers, not raises, the pressure reaching the capillaries.
Blood colloid osmotic pressure depends on plasma protein, which arteriole diameter does not change.
Arterioles are the main resistance upstream of capillaries, so their diameter directly sets capillary pressure.

why.correct: The main arterial baroreceptors are stretch-sensitive nerve endings in the wall of each carotid sinus, at the base of the internal carotid artery, and in the wall of the aortic arch. They report the pressure of blood heading to the brain and leaving the heart.
options: Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the right atrium and venae cavae sense filling and drive the atrial reflex. They are not the arterial baroreceptors.
Correct. The carotid sinuses signal through the glossopharyngeal nerves, and the aortic arch through the vagus nerves.
The medulla oblongata holds the cardiovascular center, the control center of the reflex. It receives baroreceptor signals; it does not sense arterial stretch itself.
Arterioles respond to stretch through the myogenic response, a property of their own smooth muscle. That is local control, not a sensor for the baroreceptor reflex.

why.correct: Start with MAP = CO × TPR = 4.5 × 20 = 90 mm Hg. A 20 percent fall in TPR gives 20 × 0.8 = 16 mm Hg·min/L. New MAP = 4.5 × 16 = 72 mm Hg. With cardiac output fixed, MAP falls by the same 20 percent as TPR.
options: This subtracts 20 mm Hg from the starting MAP of 90. The drop was 20 percent of TPR, not 20 mm Hg of pressure, so the new MAP is 4.5 × 16 = 72 mm Hg.
This is too small a fall. MAP is proportional to TPR when cardiac output is fixed, so a 20 percent fall in TPR gives a 20 percent fall in MAP, from 90 to 72 mm Hg.
This divides the starting MAP by 0.8, as if pressure rose when resistance fell. Lower resistance with the same flow means a lower pressure, not a higher one.

why.correct: Standing moves blood into the leg veins. Venous return, end-diastolic volume, stroke volume, cardiac output and MAP fall in a chain, and baroreceptor firing falls with MAP. That fall in firing is the signal that starts the reflex a moment later.

variables.name: Venous return
variables.why: Gravity pools blood in the stretchy veins of the legs and abdomen, so less blood reaches the right atrium.

variables.name: Stroke volume
variables.why: Less venous return means a smaller end-diastolic volume, so by the Frank–Starling mechanism each beat ejects less blood.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure
variables.why: Cardiac output falls with stroke volume, and MAP = CO × TPR, so MAP falls.

variables.name: Baroreceptor firing rate
variables.why: Lower arterial pressure stretches the carotid sinus and aortic arch walls less, so the baroreceptors fire fewer action potentials.

variables.name: Plasma protein concentration
variables.why: Pooling moves whole blood into the leg veins within seconds. It does not change what the plasma contains.

why.correct: The loop runs stimulus, sensor, afferent pathway, control center, efferent pathway and effectors, and response. The response, a rise in pressure, restores baroreceptor firing and removes the stimulus, which makes it negative feedback.

When baroreceptor firing rises, the cardiovascular center increases vagal output and reduces sympathetic output. Vagal output to the SA node rises, which is what slows the heart. The pathway says it falls, which would speed the heart and push pressure up further.
options: This step is right. Higher pressure stretches the walls where the baroreceptors sit.
This step is right. More stretch opens more mechanically gated channels in the nerve endings, so they fire faster.
This step is right. Faster firing sends more impulses along the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves to the medulla oblongata.
This is the wrong step. More baroreceptor input increases vagal output. More acetylcholine at the SA node slows the pacemaker potential and lowers heart rate.
This step is right. Less sympathetic output relaxes arteriole smooth muscle, so the arterioles widen and TPR falls.
This step is right. Lower heart rate and lower TPR reduce MAP = HR × SV × TPR, and the stimulus is removed.

why.correct: Baroreceptor input normally boosts vagal output and holds back sympathetic output. Less input does the reverse, so sympathetic output rises and vagal output falls. That is what raises heart rate and constricts the arterioles.
options: Correct. This is the control center's response to reduced baroreceptor input.
This is the response to a rise in pressure. Lower sympathetic and higher vagal output would slow the heart and widen the arterioles, lowering pressure further.
Baroreceptors are sensory neurons. They send action potentials to the brainstem; they do not release norepinephrine onto the heart. Sympathetic neurons do that.
Relaxed arterioles would lower TPR, the opposite of the result the sequence ends with.

why.correct: Norepinephrine constricts arterioles by binding alpha-1 receptors on their smooth muscle. With those blocked, TPR cannot rise when he stands, so MAP = CO × TPR stays low. His heart rate still rises, which shows the sensors, afferent nerves, control center and sympathetic output to the heart all work.
options: If the baroreceptors missed the fall, nothing would drive his heart rate up. The rise from 70 to 94 shows they did sense it.
His heart rate rose, and much of that rise comes from increased sympathetic output. The control center is responding.
The SA node responds through beta-1 receptors, which the drug does not block. His heart rate did rise.
Correct. The effector that fails is arteriole smooth muscle, because its alpha-1 receptors are blocked.

why.correct: Baroreceptors adapt. If pressure stays at a new level for a day or two, their firing settles back toward its usual rate at that level, so they stop signaling a change. This makes the reflex a fast corrector, not a setter of long-term pressure.
options: Correct. Resetting shifts the pressure the baroreceptors report as normal.
Baroreceptors fire steadily at normal pressure, so they report both rises and falls. A rise increases their firing.
Vagal output can stay raised for as long as the control center drives it. The reflex fades because its sensors reset, not because the vagus tires.
Resetting is a normal adaptation of the nerve endings over a day or two, not damage. The sinuses still work, around a new level.

why.correct: Less baroreceptor input raises sympathetic and lowers vagal output. The heart beats faster and more forcefully, arterioles in the skin, gut, kidneys and resting muscle constrict, and veins constrict and raise venous return. The brain's arterioles respond little to sympathetic signals and are controlled mainly by local autoregulation.
options: Correct. More norepinephrine and less acetylcholine at the SA node speed the pacemaker potential.
Correct. Norepinephrine on beta-1 receptors in ventricular muscle raises contractility.
Correct. Sympathetic vasoconstriction is strong in these beds, which raises TPR.
Correct. Venous constriction moves blood out of the venous reservoir, raising end-diastolic volume and stroke volume.
Brain arterioles barely respond to sympathetic signals. Local autoregulation keeps brain flow steady, and strong constriction would cut it.
Vagal output falls, not rises, when baroreceptor firing falls. Less vagal output lets heart rate climb.

why.correct: Pressing on the carotid sinus stretches its wall. The baroreceptors fire as if arterial pressure had risen, so the cardiovascular center increases vagal output, and more acetylcholine at the SA node slows the heart.
options: Blocking vagal impulses would remove the vagal brake and speed the heart, the opposite of what happened.
Brief pressure on one side leaves flow in the other carotid artery and the vertebral arteries. The heart slows because of a reflex, not because the brainstem loses blood.
Correct. The reflex reads the extra stretch as high pressure and slows the heart.
The neck is far from the right atrium, and more atrial stretch would tend to speed the heart through the atrial reflex, not slow it.

why.correct: More venous return stretches the atria and the large veins where they join. Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors there signal through the vagus nerves, the cardiovascular center raises sympathetic output to the SA node, and heart rate rises. This is the atrial (Bainbridge) reflex.
options: Arterial pressure barely changed. A rise in arterial pressure would also slow the heart through the baroreceptor reflex, not speed it.
Correct. Atrial stretch speeds the heart through the atrial reflex.
The myogenic response is arteriole smooth muscle contracting when stretched. It changes local resistance and flow, not heart rate.
Metabolic autoregulation adjusts coronary arteriole diameter to match the heart's own oxygen use. It does not set heart rate.

why.correct: While the cuff blocked flow, the forearm's cells kept working. Oxygen fell and carbon dioxide, hydrogen ions, potassium ions and adenosine built up in the interstitial fluid. These relax arteriole smooth muscle, so when the cuff came off, the arterioles were wide open and flow surged until the metabolites washed out. This is metabolic autoregulation.
options: Faster sympathetic firing would constrict the arterioles and reduce flow, not raise it. The response is local, with no nerve involved.
The arm has no baroreceptors that control its arteries. Arterial baroreceptors sit in the carotid sinuses and aortic arch and act through the brainstem.
Correct. Local metabolites dilated the arterioles, and flow stays high until the extra flow washes them away.
The myogenic response to stretch is contraction, which would narrow the arterioles and reduce flow. It cannot explain a rise in flow.

why.correct: Higher pressure stretches the arteriole wall. Stretch opens mechanically gated channels, calcium enters, and the smooth muscle contracts. The arterioles narrow and their resistance rises just enough to offset the higher pressure, so flow (ΔP / R) stays nearly the same. This is the myogenic response.
options: Correct. The myogenic response raises resistance as pressure rises.
Brain arterioles respond little to sympathetic nerves, and lower resistance with higher pressure would raise flow sharply, not hold it steady.
A wider radius would lower resistance. Combined with higher pressure, it would increase flow a lot.
Capillaries, not arterioles, are where fluid leaves the blood, and losing plasma is not how flow is held steady. Arterioles control flow by changing their radius.

why.correct: In exercise, the nervous system raises cardiac output while working muscle dilates its own arterioles. Because cardiac output rises several-fold and TPR falls by less, MAP rises a little. Flow is shifted from the gut and kidneys to muscle. Brain flow changes little, so the brain's share of the much larger output falls.

variables.name: Cardiac output
variables.why: Sympathetic stimulation and vagal withdrawal raise heart rate, and higher contractility plus the skeletal muscle pump raise stroke volume.

variables.name: Total peripheral resistance
variables.why: Metabolites in working muscle dilate its many arterioles. That fall outweighs sympathetic vasoconstriction in the gut and kidneys.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure
variables.why: Cardiac output rises more than TPR falls, so their product rises, but only modestly.

variables.name: Blood flow to the gut
variables.why: Sympathetic vasoconstriction narrows the gut's arterioles, and it has no metabolites strong enough to override it.

variables.name: Share of cardiac output going to the brain
variables.why: Local autoregulation keeps brain flow roughly constant while cardiac output rises several-fold, so the brain gets a smaller share of the total.

why.correct: Maximum heart rate = 220 − 50 = 170 beats/min. Then 0.70 × 170 = 119 and 0.85 × 170 = 144.5, which rounds to 145. The zone is about 119 to 145 beats/min.
options: This is 50 to 70 percent of 170, the moderate zone, not the vigorous one.
This is the vigorous zone for a 40-year-old, whose estimated maximum is 180. It uses the wrong age.
This subtracts 30 and 0 beats from the maximum instead of taking percentages of it.

why.correct: MAP = CO × TPR = 15 × 7 = 105 mm Hg. Resting MAP was 5 × 18 = 90 mm Hg. Cardiac output tripled, but TPR fell to less than half, so MAP rose by only about 17 percent.
options: This is the resting MAP, 5 × 18. During the run both cardiac output and TPR have changed.
Correct. 15 × 7 = 105 mm Hg.
This multiplies the running cardiac output by the resting TPR. It ignores the fall in resistance as muscle arterioles dilate, which is what keeps pressure from soaring.
This multiplies the resting TPR by 7 instead of multiplying the running cardiac output by the running TPR.

why.correct: The immediate change is a fall in venous return, cardiac output and MAP, sensed as reduced baroreceptor firing. Within a minute the reflex raises heart rate, contractility, venous tone and TPR. MAP climbs back toward normal, at the cost of lower flow to the skin and gut, while the brain and heart keep their flow.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure, first few seconds
variables.why: Less blood volume means less venous return, a smaller stroke volume and lower cardiac output, so MAP = CO × TPR falls.

variables.name: Baroreceptor firing, first few seconds
variables.why: Lower arterial pressure stretches the carotid sinus and aortic arch walls less.

variables.name: Heart rate, one minute later
variables.why: The cardiovascular center raises sympathetic output and lowers vagal output to the SA node.

variables.name: Total peripheral resistance, one minute later
variables.why: Norepinephrine on alpha-1 receptors constricts arterioles in the skin, gut, kidneys and resting muscle.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure one minute later, compared with its lowest point
variables.why: Higher heart rate, contractility, venous tone and TPR push MAP back up toward normal.

variables.name: Blood flow to the skin, one minute later
variables.why: Skin arterioles constrict strongly under sympathetic stimulation, which is why a bleeding person looks pale and feels cool.

why.correct: Long-standing diabetes can damage autonomic nerves. Her pressure falls, yet neither heart rate nor resistance rises. That points to the efferent pathway: the sympathetic signals never reach the SA node and the arterioles, so the reflex cannot respond.
options: Nothing points to glucose blocking baroreceptor channels. Autonomic nerve damage is the well-known complication of long-standing diabetes.
Correct. Damaged sympathetic efferent nerves leave the heart and arterioles unable to respond, so both heart rate and TPR stay flat.
Her veins still pool blood on standing; that pooling is what lowers her pressure. The problem is the missing reflex response to it.
Autoregulation protects brain flow, but it cannot raise systemic pressure or heart rate. Her unchanged heart rate points to a problem in the reflex, not in local control.

why.correct: Brain arterioles respond little to sympathetic vasoconstriction and are controlled mainly by local autoregulation, which holds flow steady over a wide range of pressure. The heart is protected in the same way.
options: Skin arterioles constrict strongly under sympathetic stimulation, so skin flow falls early and a lot.
The gut's arterioles constrict strongly, so gut flow falls, shifting blood toward the brain and heart.
Kidney arterioles constrict under sympathetic stimulation, so kidney flow falls.
Correct. Local autoregulation, not sympathetic signals, controls brain flow.

why.correct: Orthostatic hypotension is a sustained fall of at least 20 mm Hg systolic or at least 10 mm Hg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing.
options: A small fall of a few mm Hg is normal in the first seconds of standing and is corrected by the reflex.
A rise of 10 to 20 beats/min is the normal reflex response to standing, not a failure of it.
Many healthy people have a systolic pressure below 120. The definition is based on the fall on standing, not on one reading.
Correct. Either criterion is enough.

why.correct: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) sits on the surface of endothelial cells and is most plentiful in the capillaries of the lungs, which all of your cardiac output passes through. It converts angiotensin I into the active hormone, angiotensin II.
options: Renin makes angiotensin I from angiotensinogen. It acts one step earlier and does not make angiotensin II.
Correct. ACE, mostly in the lungs, makes angiotensin II.
Angiotensinogen is the inactive protein that renin cuts, not an enzyme that converts angiotensin I.
Aldosterone is a hormone released because of angiotensin II. It is not an enzyme in the cascade.

why.correct: 2.9 g ÷ 58.5 g/mol ≈ 0.05 mol, or 50 mmol of sodium. Thirst and ADH add water until that sodium sits at the normal 140 mmol/L. 50 ÷ 140 ≈ 0.36 L of extra fluid outside the cells.
options: This is the amount of salt in moles, 0.05 mol, not a volume of fluid. The next step is to divide 50 mmol by 140 mmol/L.
This divides 140 by 50 instead of 50 by 140. Holding 50 mmol at 140 mmol/L needs less than half a liter.
This is about a fifth of 0.36 L, the part that ends up in the plasma, not the whole extra volume outside the cells.
Correct. 50 mmol ÷ 140 mmol/L ≈ 0.36 L.

why.correct: The infusion raises blood volume and venous return, which stretches the atria. Stretched atrial muscle cells release ANP. ANP makes the kidneys excrete more sodium and water and reduces renin, aldosterone and ADH, so the extra volume is gradually removed.
options: Higher volume and pressure reduce renin and so angiotensin II, which lowers aldosterone. The kidneys keep less sodium, not more.
Correct. Atrial stretch releases ANP, which drives sodium and water into the urine.
Renin falls when pressure in the kidney's small arteries rises. More volume means less renin.
Saline has the same concentration as plasma, so osmolarity does not rise, and the rise in volume lowers ADH.

why.correct: Water loss raises osmolarity and lowers volume. The nervous system, the kidneys, the adrenal cortex, the hypothalamus and the heart all respond: ADH, renin and aldosterone rise, ANP falls, and her kidneys make a small volume of concentrated urine while she waits for a drink.

variables.name: Plasma osmolarity
variables.why: She lost more water than salt, so the solutes left in her plasma are more concentrated.

variables.name: ADH release
variables.why: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors sense the higher osmolarity, and the fall in volume adds to the signal.

variables.name: Renin release
variables.why: Lower pressure in the kidney's small arteries and more sympathetic stimulation both increase renin release.

variables.name: Aldosterone
variables.why: More renin means more angiotensin II, which makes the adrenal cortex release aldosterone.

variables.name: ANP release
variables.why: With less blood volume, venous return falls and the atria are stretched less.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: ADH makes the kidneys keep water, and aldosterone makes them keep sodium, which water follows.

why.correct: Low pressure is sensed in the kidney, which releases renin. Renin forms angiotensin I from angiotensinogen, ACE converts it to angiotensin II, angiotensin II releases aldosterone, and aldosterone makes the kidneys keep sodium, which water follows.
Angiotensin II stimulates the adrenal cortex, so aldosterone release rises, not falls. Aldosterone is what makes the kidneys keep sodium in the last step.
options: This step is right. The baroreceptor reflex raises sympathetic output when pressure falls, and that output reaches the renin-making cells.
This step is right. Norepinephrine on beta-1 receptors and less stretch both increase renin release.
This step is right. More renin makes more angiotensin I, which ACE converts to angiotensin II.
This is the wrong step. Angiotensin II increases aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex.
This step is right. Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption, and water follows by osmosis.

why.correct: With ACE blocked, less angiotensin II is made. Arterioles relax, and the adrenal cortex releases less aldosterone, so the kidneys keep less sodium and water. Blood volume and TPR both fall, which lowers pressure.
options: Angiotensin II normally holds back renin release. With less angiotensin II and lower pressure, renin release rises.
Angiotensin I is made by renin, which still works. With the conversion step blocked, angiotensin I builds up.
Correct. Less angiotensin II means less aldosterone, so more sodium and water leave in the urine.
Aldosterone makes the kidneys secrete potassium. With less aldosterone, they secrete less, so plasma potassium tends to rise.

why.correct: Sodium stays mostly outside cells, so fluid kept with sodium stays in the plasma and interstitial fluid. Pure water dilutes every compartment and moves into the cells by osmosis, so only a small fraction of it remains in the blood.
options: The lungs lose water as vapor at a steady rate that does not depend on what you drink, and they do not excrete a drink.
Sodium does not change the size of plasma proteins or their osmotic pull.
Water crosses capillary walls freely through the clefts between endothelial cells, and it is absorbed from the gut.
Correct. Water follows solute. Sodium keeps its water outside the cells; pure water spreads everywhere.

why.correct: A fall in volume of more than about 5 to 10 percent reduces stretch of the arterial baroreceptors and of the stretch sensors in the atria and large veins. That drives ADH release steeply, to levels far above those osmolarity produces, and the volume signal overrides a normal osmolarity.
options: Losing whole blood removes plasma and its solutes together, so osmolarity stays normal. The osmoreceptors are not the source of this signal.
Correct. A large volume loss is a powerful ADH trigger in its own right.
Pain and stress can raise ADH somewhat, but the rise after a large bleed is driven mainly by the loss of volume.
ADH comes from hypothalamic neurons and is released from the posterior pituitary. The kidneys are its target, not its source.

why.correct: Angiotensin II raises pressure on several fronts: it constricts arterioles, releases aldosterone, triggers thirst and ADH release, and makes the kidneys keep sodium directly. ANP is released by atrial stretch, and it works against angiotensin II.
options: Correct. This is the fast arm, acting within minutes.
Correct. Aldosterone is the slow arm, raising volume over hours to days.
Correct. Angiotensin II acts on the hypothalamus.
ANP release is triggered by atrial stretch, not angiotensin II. ANP opposes the RAAS.
Angiotensin II makes the kidneys keep sodium, both directly and through aldosterone. Excreting sodium is what ANP promotes.

why.correct: ANP makes the kidneys excrete more sodium, and water leaves with it. It also lowers renin, aldosterone and ADH. The lost fluid lowers blood volume, which reduces atrial stretch.
options: Correct. Natriuresis, with water following, is the step that lowers volume.
ANP reduces aldosterone release. More aldosterone would make the kidneys keep sodium and raise volume.
ANP reduces ADH release. More ADH would make the kidneys keep water.
ANP relaxes arteriole smooth muscle, lowering TPR. Constriction is the opposite of its effect.

why.correct: Adding fluid that matches plasma raises volume but not osmolarity. The atria sense the extra volume and release ANP, the RAAS switches down, and the kidneys excrete the extra sodium and water over the next hours.

variables.name: Atrial stretch
variables.why: More blood volume raises venous return, which fills and stretches the atria more.

variables.name: ANP release
variables.why: Stretched atrial muscle cells release ANP.

variables.name: Renin release
variables.why: Higher pressure in the kidney's small arteries, less sympathetic stimulation and ANP all reduce renin release.

variables.name: Aldosterone
variables.why: Less renin means less angiotensin II, and ANP also reduces aldosterone release directly.

variables.name: Plasma osmolarity
variables.why: Saline matches the concentration of plasma, so it adds volume without changing osmolarity.

variables.name: Urine sodium excretion
variables.why: More ANP and less aldosterone make the kidneys keep less sodium, so more leaves in the urine with water.

why.correct: Her fast heart and constricted arterioles hold pressure up for now, but they do not replace the lost fluid, and the baroreceptors reset over a day or two. Lasting correction comes from blood volume: with RAAS and ADH switched on, her kidneys keep the salt and water she drinks until volume is restored.
options: Baroreceptors reset within a day or two, so the reflex cannot hold heart rate up indefinitely, and a faster heart does not replace lost fluid.
Constriction raises TPR and holds pressure up in the short term, but it does not restore the missing volume.
Correct. Under RAAS and ADH, her kidneys keep sodium and water, and long-term control works by restoring blood volume.
Low volume reduces atrial stretch, so ANP falls. ANP also lowers volume, the opposite of what she needs.

why.correct: Excess aldosterone makes the kidneys keep sodium, with water following, so volume and pressure rise. It also makes them secrete potassium, so plasma potassium falls. The higher pressure stretches the renin-making cells, so renin release falls.
options: Correct. Volume rises, potassium falls, and negative feedback turns renin down.
This is the pattern of too little aldosterone. Extra aldosterone keeps sodium and water and removes potassium.
Potassium falls with extra aldosterone, and the higher pressure turns renin down, not up.
Extra aldosterone keeps sodium and water, so volume rises rather than falls.

why.correct: Right after the bleed, pressure falls and the reflex speeds the heart. Over the next hours, renin, angiotensin II, aldosterone and ADH rise, urine output falls and thirst increases. Over one to two days, kept and drunk fluid restores plasma volume, so the fast reflex no longer has to work hard and heart rate settles.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure, first minutes
variables.why: Less volume means less venous return, stroke volume and cardiac output, so MAP falls before the reflexes fully catch up.

variables.name: Renin release, first hour
variables.why: Lower pressure in the kidney's small arteries and sympathetic stimulation of the renin-making cells both increase renin.

variables.name: ADH, first hour
variables.why: A loss of this size lowers stretch of the baroreceptors and the atrial sensors, which drives ADH release steeply.

variables.name: Urine volume, first day
variables.why: Aldosterone keeps sodium and ADH keeps water, so less of both reaches the urine.

variables.name: Plasma volume two days later, compared with just after the bleed
variables.why: Kept salt and water, plus thirst-driven drinking, refill the plasma.

variables.name: Heart rate two days later, compared with the first hour
variables.why: With volume restored, venous return and stroke volume recover, baroreceptor firing returns, and sympathetic drive to the SA node eases.
