why.correct: The renin-making cells are stretch-sensitive. Higher pressure stretches them more, and they release less renin. This is the negative feedback that switches the RAAS off once pressure recovers.
options: Lower pressure means less stretch of the renin-making cells, which increases renin release.
Norepinephrine on beta-1 receptors of the renin-making cells increases renin release.
Less salt reaching the sensing cells makes them signal for more renin, not less.
Correct. More stretch reduces renin release.

why.correct: Extra volume stretches the atria, so ANP rises. It also raises pressure in the kidney's small arteries, and ANP itself inhibits renin, so renin and angiotensin II fall, and aldosterone falls with them. Every signal pushes the kidneys to excrete sodium and water.
options: Renin and aldosterone rise when volume is low. With extra volume and high ANP, both are turned down.
This is the pattern for low volume. Extra volume raises ANP and lowers renin and aldosterone.
Correct. High ANP with low renin and aldosterone is the response to too much volume.
ANP is released by atrial stretch, which extra volume increases, so ANP would be high, not low.

why.correct: ANP is released by muscle cells in the atrial walls when more venous return stretches them.
options: Low pressure in the kidney releases renin, not ANP.
Correct. Atrial stretch releases ANP.
Angiotensin II makes the adrenal cortex release aldosterone, not ANP.
Hypothalamic neurons make ADH, which is released when osmolarity rises.

why.correct: The water dilutes the plasma. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus sense even a 1 to 2 percent fall in osmolarity and reduce ADH release. With little ADH, the kidneys keep less water, so a large volume of dilute urine follows.
options: Correct. Less ADH means the kidneys keep less water.
Most of the water moves into the cells, so blood volume rises only slightly, and nowhere near doubles. The main signal is the fall in osmolarity.
Plain water lowers osmolarity rather than raising it, and more ADH would make urine smaller and more concentrated.
Extra fluid does not increase renin, and more aldosterone would make the kidneys keep sodium and water, not excrete them.

why.correct: Shock is a failure of the circulation to deliver enough oxygen for the tissues' needs. Cells then switch to anaerobic metabolism and lactate rises. Blood pressure may still be near normal while reflexes compensate.
options: Low pressure is common in shock, but it is often a late sign. A patient can be in shock with a pressure that reflexes are still holding up.
Correct. The definition is about oxygen delivery, not a pressure number.
Fainting is a brief loss of consciousness from reduced brain flow, often on standing. It is not the same as shock.
A fast heart rate is an early sign of shock, but many things raise heart rate, and it does not define shock.

why.correct: Systolic 136 falls in the 130 to 139 range, which is stage 1. Diastolic 78 is normal, but when the two numbers fall in different categories, the higher category counts. The reading is stage 1 hypertension.
options: Normal needs a systolic below 120 and a diastolic below 80. A systolic of 136 is well above that.
Elevated covers systolic 120 to 129 with diastolic below 80. A systolic of 136 is above that range.
Stage 2 starts at 140 systolic or 90 diastolic. Neither number reaches that.
Correct. The systolic value of 136 places the reading in stage 1.

why.correct: Immediately, the loss of whole blood lowers volume without changing blood's makeup. Within minutes the reflex speeds the heart and constricts arterioles. Over hours, fluid moves into the plasma and dilutes it, and the kidneys keep salt and water. Over weeks, EPO rebuilds the red cells.

variables.name: Hematocrit, first minutes
variables.why: Whole blood was lost, cells and plasma together, so the fraction made of red cells has not changed yet.

variables.name: Heart rate, ten minutes later
variables.why: Lower MAP reduces baroreceptor firing, so sympathetic output to the SA node rises and vagal output falls.

variables.name: Pulse pressure, ten minutes later
variables.why: Stroke volume is smaller, which lowers systolic pressure, while arteriole constriction holds diastolic pressure up.

variables.name: Hematocrit, eight hours later
variables.why: Low capillary pressure first drew interstitial fluid into the plasma. Then filtration stayed below the drainage returning fluid, so cell-free fluid kept being added, diluting the remaining red cells.

variables.name: Urine output, first day
variables.why: Aldosterone makes the kidneys keep sodium and the high ADH makes them keep water.

variables.name: Red blood cell count, three weeks later compared with the first day
variables.why: Lower oxygen delivery to the kidneys raised EPO, which drives red blood cell production in the red bone marrow.

why.correct: This is septic shock, a form of distributive shock. Signals released in response to the infection, including cytokines and nitric oxide, dilate vessels throughout the body. TPR falls sharply, and early on the skin is warm because blood flows freely to it.
options: In hypovolemic shock, reflex constriction makes the skin cool and pale, and fluids restore pressure. Her warm skin and poor response to fluids point elsewhere.
Correct. Low TPR from widespread vasodilation is the core problem in septic shock.
A failing pump causes cardiogenic shock, with cool skin from reflex constriction. Early in sepsis, cardiac output is often high.
An obstruction causes obstructive shock, with cool skin and high venous pressure. Nothing here suggests a blockage.

why.correct: This is neurogenic shock. The injury cuts the sympathetic pathways that run down the spinal cord from the brainstem, so arterioles and veins lose their tone and dilate, and the heart loses its sympathetic drive. The vagus nerve leaves the brainstem directly and is untouched, so unopposed vagal output keeps the heart rate low.
options: The baroreceptors and their nerves (IX and X) run outside the spinal cord and still signal the fall in pressure. The problem is that the response cannot travel down the cord.
Nothing suggests a higher blood volume. The low pressure comes from loss of vessel tone, which pools blood in dilated veins.
Correct. Loss of sympathetic output with intact vagal output explains the slow heart and warm, dry skin.
The SA node is in the heart, far from the injury. It is working, under the control of the vagus nerve alone.

why.correct: A large infarct leaves the left ventricle too weak to pump out what the lungs deliver. Cardiac output falls, which is cardiogenic shock. Pressure rises in the left atrium and lung capillaries, and fluid filters into the lung tissue and air spaces, causing the crackles.
options: Correct. A failing pump with high filling pressure behind it is cardiogenic shock.
An infarct does not bleed away enough blood to cause hypovolemic shock, and low volume would leave the lungs dry, not wet.
His cool, clammy skin shows reflex vasoconstriction, not widespread vasodilation. The lung fluid comes from high capillary pressure.
A clot in the pulmonary trunk would cause obstructive shock but would not back fluid up into the lungs, which lie beyond the right ventricle's outflow.

why.correct: Blood collecting in the pericardial cavity (cardiac tamponade) presses on the heart, so the ventricles cannot fill. Blood backs up in the systemic veins, making the jugular veins bulge, and cardiac output falls. This is obstructive shock.
options: Blood loss would leave the neck veins flat, because venous pressure falls. His bulging veins show blood backing up.
A weak left ventricle would back fluid into the lungs, but his lungs are clear. The problem is filling, not pumping strength.
Pain raises sympathetic output and constricts arterioles; it does not cause widespread dilation. Bulging neck veins do not fit that picture.
Correct. Tamponade prevents filling, which is obstructive shock.

why.correct: A left ventricle damaged by the infarct cannot pump out all that the lungs deliver. Pressure backs up into the left atrium, pulmonary veins and lung capillaries, and fluid filters into the lungs. Lying flat returns more blood from the legs to the chest and worsens it.
options: Right-sided failure backs blood up into the systemic veins and causes ankle swelling and bulging neck veins, not wet lungs. Her ankles are normal.
Correct. Breathlessness when lying flat and crackles in the lungs point to left-sided failure.
She shows no signs of shock or blood loss. The fluid in her lungs is filtered plasma, not lost blood.
Distributive shock lowers pressure throughout the body. Her problem is a backlog of blood behind a weak left ventricle.

why.correct: The right ventricle cannot pump out all the blood that returns to it, so pressure rises in the systemic veins. Venous pressure passes back into the capillaries, raising capillary hydrostatic pressure. More fluid filters out than drains away, and gravity pulls it to the ankles.
options: Albumin is usually normal in heart failure. The swelling comes from high capillary pressure.
The capillary wall is not unusually leaky here. The extra filtration is driven by pressure.
Correct. Backed-up venous pressure raises capillary pressure and filtration.
Lower arteriole pressure would reduce capillary pressure and filtration, which would not cause swelling.

why.correct: A weak left ventricle lowers stroke volume and backs blood up into the lungs. The nervous system and the kidneys read the low output as low pressure: sympathetic output, renin, aldosterone and ADH rise, and blood volume grows. The extra volume raises filling pressures further, worsening congestion.

variables.name: Stroke volume
variables.why: A weaker ventricle ejects less blood with each beat, and its flattened Frank–Starling curve limits any rise from more filling.

variables.name: Pressure in the lung capillaries
variables.why: Blood the left ventricle cannot eject backs up into the left atrium and pulmonary veins.

variables.name: Renin release
variables.why: Lower cardiac output lowers pressure in the kidney's small arteries, and sympathetic stimulation adds to renin release.

variables.name: Blood volume
variables.why: Aldosterone and ADH make the kidneys keep salt and water.

variables.name: Sympathetic output to the heart and arterioles
variables.why: Lower cardiac output reduces baroreceptor firing, so the cardiovascular center raises sympathetic output.

variables.name: ANP release
variables.why: Higher filling pressures stretch the atria, so they release more ANP, though not enough to offset the RAAS.

why.correct: Resistance varies with 1 / radius⁴. The ratio of new to old resistance is (3 ÷ 2)⁴ = 1.5⁴ = 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.5 ≈ 5.06. A one-third cut in radius makes resistance about 5 times higher.
options: This uses the radius ratio, 1.5, without raising it to the fourth power.
This squares the ratio (1.5² ≈ 2.25). Resistance depends on the fourth power, not the second.
Correct. 1.5⁴ ≈ 5.
This raises 3 to the fourth power instead of the ratio 3 ÷ 2.

why.correct: Endothelial injury lets cholesterol-carrying particles into the intima. Macrophages engulf them and become foam cells, smooth muscle cells build a fibrous cap, and a thin cap can rupture. Platelets then build a thrombus that can block the artery.

The kidneys keep salt and water as if pressure were low. A failing ventricle sits on the flat part of its Frank–Starling curve, so more filling adds little stroke volume. The extra volume mostly raises venous and capillary pressures, worsening fluid in the lungs and tissues.
options: Correct. More filling brings more congestion and little extra output.
Retained fluid dilutes the blood only mildly. The main harm is higher pressure behind the failing pump.
Heart failure raises sympathetic output and heart rate. The baroreceptor reflex is not switched off by extra volume.
In heart failure TPR rises, from sympathetic stimulation and angiotensin II. It does not fall.

why.correct: In compensated hypovolemic shock, sympathetic output raises heart rate and constricts the skin's arterioles. Diastolic pressure is held up while stroke volume falls, so pulse pressure narrows. The RAAS and ADH make the kidneys keep salt and water, so urine output falls.
options: Correct. The baroreceptor reflex speeds the heart.
Correct. Skin arterioles constrict, and sympathetic stimulation of sweat glands makes the skin clammy.
Correct. Systolic pressure falls with stroke volume while vasoconstriction holds diastolic pressure up.
Correct. Aldosterone and ADH reduce the loss of salt and water in urine.
Warm, flushed skin means dilated skin vessels, as in early septic shock. In blood loss the skin vessels constrict.
A slow heart rate is expected in neurogenic shock, not in blood loss, where the reflex speeds the heart.

why.correct: Heart muscle starved of oxygen contracts more weakly, so contractility falls, not rises. That fall in contractility lowers cardiac output, which lowers pressure and coronary flow further: a positive feedback loop.
options: This step is right. Progressive shock begins when compensation can no longer hold MAP up.
This step is right. Coronary flow depends on aortic pressure, so it falls when MAP falls.
This step is right. Less coronary flow delivers less oxygen to the heart muscle.
This is the wrong step. Ischemic heart muscle makes less ATP and contracts more weakly.
This step is right. Weaker contraction lowers stroke volume and cardiac output, closing the loop.

why.correct: A young, elastic aorta stretches as the ventricle ejects, absorbing part of each surge. With age the aorta stiffens, so the same stroke volume raises pressure more during systole, and there is less stored recoil to hold pressure up in diastole. Systolic pressure rises and pulse pressure widens.
options: A slow heart rate lengthens diastole, not shortens it, and would not explain a high systolic value.
Correct. Arterial stiffening raises systolic pressure and widens pulse pressure.
Low volume would lower pressures, not raise systolic pressure to 168.
Lower TPR would lower pressure, especially diastolic, and would not raise systolic pressure.

why.correct: With capillary pressure below the inward oncotic pull, fluid moves from the interstitial spaces into the capillaries for a few minutes. After that, filtration stays below its old rate while drainage keeps returning fluid, so the plasma keeps gaining fluid for hours. That fluid has no red cells, so it dilutes the remaining cells and hematocrit falls.
options: Marrow output does not drop after a bleed; EPO rises and increases it over days. The hours-long fall in hematocrit is dilution.
After a bleed, ADH and aldosterone make the kidneys keep water, not excrete it.
Red blood cells are far too large to pass through the clefts between endothelial cells.
Correct. Protein-poor, cell-free fluid added to the plasma lowers hematocrit.

why.correct: With higher arterial pressure, the left ventricle must generate more pressure to open the aortic valve and eject. That extra work makes its muscle cells enlarge (hypertrophy), so the wall thickens. A thick wall is stiff, fills poorly and needs more oxygen.
options: Correct. Pressure overload from a higher afterload thickens the ventricle.
Hypertension does not lower preload, and a lower preload would not build new muscle.
Hypertension is not an infection and does not cause one. The thickening is an adaptation to extra work.
ANP comes mainly from the atria and does not make cardiac muscle cells divide. Adult cardiac muscle cells enlarge rather than divide.

why.correct: Blood loss has lowered his stroke volume, but the baroreceptor reflex is holding MAP up with a fast heart and strong arteriole constriction. The narrow pulse pressure (22 mm Hg) and cool, clammy skin show how hard the reflex is working. This is compensated hypovolemic shock, and it can progress quickly if bleeding continues.
options: Shock is defined by oxygen delivery, not a pressure number. His fast heart, narrow pulse pressure and cool skin are early signs of shock.
Widespread vasodilation would make his skin warm and his diastolic pressure low. His cool skin and high diastolic pressure show constriction.
Correct. His reflexes are compensating for the lost volume.
A narrow pulse pressure is an early sign of compensation, not a sign of irreversible damage. He is alert enough to talk and still compensating.

why.correct: A sudden blockage at rest usually comes from plaque rupture. The fibrous cap cracks, blood meets the fatty core, platelets stick, and a thrombus forms within minutes and blocks the artery.
options: Plaques grow over years, not in a single morning. A sudden event points to rupture and a thrombus.
Correct. Cap rupture triggers a thrombus that blocks the artery suddenly.
Spasm can narrow a coronary artery, but a fall in blood pressure relaxes arteries rather than making them spasm. Rupture with a thrombus is the usual cause.
Cholesterol does not dissolve in blood. When plaque contents are exposed, the result is a clot, not dissolved cholesterol.

why.correct: When the left ventricle fails, pressure backs up into the lungs. The right ventricle must then pump against a higher pressure in the pulmonary circuit, and over time it fails too.
options: A low-salt diet lowers blood volume and filling pressure. It does not damage the right ventricle.
Low blood volume lowers filling pressures. It causes hypovolemic shock, not heart failure.
An enlarged liver is a result of right-sided failure, as blood backs up into the systemic veins, not its cause.
Correct. Left-sided failure raises the pressure the right ventricle must pump against.
